['There are a few scenarios here that I could imagine following your line of thinking :

1. If a developer wants to enable Agent A to call a known Agent B at design time, Agent A can be told what schema Agent B needs for calling arguments. Agent A can just hardcode and there's no need to describe the schema in Agent B's Agent Card.

2. Agent A discovers Agent B at runtime and wants to make a call, so it investigates Agent B Agent Card and reads a JSON Schema included somewhere in the card.  However, Agent A doesn't know the semantics of that JSON Schema. It only knows that it needs to send some JSON.  So Agent A is going to have to use an LLM to infer the JSON values based on the schema and the context and the model's knowledge of the JSON key names.  We have a protocol that does exactly that. MCP.  I'm not convinced we should replicate MCP capability in A2A.

3.  Consider a third scenario.  Agent A calls the newly discovered Agent B and sends a message to Agent B that describes the problem that it is trying to solve using natural language.  Agent B responds with a message that provides a JSON Schema, or some other description of the parameters  that are appropriate for either the advanced skill or the basic skill depending on which Agent B thinks is more appropriate.  Agent A formulates the JSON structure, using an LLM, based on the JSON schema shared by Agent B and makes the call.
That initial handshake interaction between Agent A and Agent B is potentially expensive because it requires that extra LLM call from Agent B to understand the intent.  That is part of the price that we pay for being able to dynamically discover agents.  However, that negotiation doesn't need to happen every time Agent A needs to talk to Agent B.  Agent A is free to cache that parameter schema and reuse it again for similar questions it may have in the future.

Honestly, we are all walking into new territory here, but I personally don't think that A2A is just different shaped tool calling.  A2A offers us the opportunity to rethink how we enable agents to negotiate how to interact effectively.  I don't think trying cram all that information into the AgentCard is actually going to move us significantly forward.  If you want predefined JSON Schema based tool calls, MCP has got you covered.

This is part of the reason why Skills are "hand wavy" descriptions that say an agent can do these kind of things.  They are not trying to be a new interface definition language.  The agent card does support declaring input and output media types.  Personally, I believe these are an mechanism that can be used to provide precisely defined ways to share well understood content.  These are not intended for generic media types like "application/json" but for media types that have rich semantics like "text/calendar".  The important distinction is that media types are not generally designed for one specific API or agent.  They are designed to be reused across many different applications.  The talk I gave at A2A Summit goes into this topic in some more detail with some examples.  Hopefully that will be available soon.', '@chorghemaruti64-creator 

> A capability-aware discovery layer helps here: agents could declare in their card/manifest which auth patterns they support (OAuth2, API key, out-of-band, etc.) and whether AUTH_REQUIRED is possible mid-task vs only at initiation. Clients can then make informed decisions before starting a long-running task — rather than discovering the auth requirement partway through.

This is something that I've seen requested before. It would be a convenient feature to ensure that the agent has all necessary credentials before it begins work, which can prevent Tasks from getting stuck waiting for authorization. There is room for this in the protocol, but this area is tricky enough I've been expecting to explore it via extensions first. Concretely implementing and validating the design gives us much more confidence that it's the right thing to do.

For example, should clients always attempt to provide the maximal amount of credentials to the agent? If not, how should they correlate the agent's declared credential requirements with the task they delegate to the agent? Must agents declare all their possible credentials, or is it optional? Does it compose well with chains of multiple agents?

I have thought about this problem before and feel that we need two components:

1. A way for an agent to declare what outbound credentials it may need for each skill.
2. A way for a client and agent to agree upon an execution plan for a Task. This plan can include the set of credentials needed. Clients can then provide all necessary credentials (somehow, this is not currently defined in the base A2A spec) when it agrees and requests execution of the plan.

If you'd like, feel free to file a separate issue for tracking your request. This issue is specifically about what the client/server expectations are for Tasks that enter `TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED` and `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED`.

@darrelmiller 

> Thinking more about this, it might not be a naive implementation, it might be a very efficient approach. Why keep a stream open, when you have no idea how long it might take for a client to address the input_required state? If the user has walked away from their desk, then it could be hours/days.

> Anytime it wants. A client can always subscribe again. However, it would be a very unhelpful A2A server that reduced streaming into polling because it continuously shut down the stream.

Agreed it is efficient and should be allowed. What I'd like to make sure we clarify is the expectations for clients and how they should handle these cases. Extrapolating from what you've laid out here, it sounds like clients should essentially endlessly attempt to reconnect to the stream when they see it terminate before the Task is in a terminal state. Servers are free to end this stream immediately if there is no active agent working on the Task, and so a client should not consider the stream closing as an error.

> Not a conflict. We don't want to make it a conflict because we don't want the server to have to start tracking that case. Imagine having to check to see if there is a live stream with a client listening before you can accept a message. A client can open 10 SendStreamingMessage streams and still SendMessages, the agent shouldn't care.

> I think this is less about tracking streams and more a question "what happens if I SendMessage to a Task in different states?" i.e. if a Task is WORKING vs INPUT_REQUIRED etc, and if two clients see INPUT_REQUIRED for the same Task and both SendMessage concurrently how should this be handled. (We currently don't have eTags or anything like that to prevent lost updates)

Yes to Sam's points. As I see it, if an agent is actively working through a request and the A2A server receives a new request, the server has a few options for how it could handle this:

1. The A2A handler enqueues the message for the next time the agent is ready to receive inputs, meaning the message is only read once the current stream of processing has concluded.
2. The A2A handler interrupts the agent processing, feeding the agent the new event as the start of a new processing loop.
3. The A2A handler returns a Conflict error indicating the agent is currently processing and can't handle this request
4. The A2A handler doesn't detect anything and just starts running the agent with the most recent Task state.

Strategy 1 requires agents to have a queue of inputs and it's unclear what the client should expect to see. Does the request block until the agent consumes the message? Does it just act like a SubscribeToTask, where you get the current stream of events? If so, how do you know when the agent has actually read your message? I think we'd need some kind of tracking for how outputs correlate to input messages, such as sequence numbers ("this is output event 17 that was based off of input sequence ID 1 -> this is output 18 that was based off of input sequence ID 2 -> great, you saw my message").

Strategy 2 is clearer on the client side, but puts a requirement that you can interrupt an agent. If an agent emits an event after the interrupting request was received, should it be dropped? Probably not, since the event may indicate that something changed in the session/external state, but then we're back to the same question above: if you send a message to a task that's actively processing, and you receive an event in response, is that event related to your message or just from whatever was happening before?

Strategy 3 is the clearest. If it's not safe to interrupt an agent, or this has not been implemented, or the server can't enqueue messages, it just returns a Conflict. But the client should probably have some idea of when it _is_ safe to send a message. The protocol should probably safeguard that a client should always be able to send a message when the Task is in `TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED`. The induced requirement is that either an agent always pauses execution after entering that state, or that the agent has some means of enqueuing the message or interrupting the agent when a message is received. We don't require that a server can receive a message in any other Task state (except perhaps `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED`).

Strategy 4 is broken, but is what happens if you directly link your agent execution to the A2A request lifecycle. I state it here to be clear that certain requirements are already present for how to implement an A2A server -- you must at least track whether you are actively processing the task and producing updates somewhere.

I think in v2 of the protocol we should consider disentangling TaskState from input and auth-required. We could elevate a request for input or authorization to direct Task artifacts (not capital-A Artifacts), and switch the TaskState to `blocked`, with the ability to say "I'm blocked until request X is addressed". This allows explicitly indicating "I need this input, but I can continue working for now." It also allows having multiple outstanding input or auth requests. The blocked state would indicate "there's nothing going on right now, come back later" and also "it's safe to send me a message". There's still a question of how a client is supposed to know when something will start happening, but one option is to interpret that as an explicit signal to switch to webhooks.', '## **Background**

This document outlines a design for how agent-to-agent (A2A) systems should handle scenarios where a client needs to follow up on or refine a previously completed task.

## **Proposal**
Tasks cannot be restarted from terminal states (e.g., Completed, Failed, Cancelled). Clients can refer previous Tasks for followups or refinements. Implemented in #608 

## **Design**


### **Option 1: Restartable Tasks**

This option proposes that agents allow tasks to be restarted from terminal states (e.g., Completed, Failed, Cancelled).

**Pros:**



*   **Simpler Context Handling:** Agent developers wouldn't need to manage broader context from a contextID, as they could use the local context from the original task.
*   **Easier Event Tracking:** Simplifies tracking the sequence of events that lead to a final artifact.

**Cons:**



*   **Breaks Client-Task Mapping:** A mutable task breaks the one-to-one mapping between a client's planning node and a single task execution, as a "completed" task could be modified later.
*   **Difficult Bookkeeping:** It becomes harder to track the work done by an agent, as multiple instructions are combined into a single task.
*   **Client Ambiguity:** The client has an ambiguous choice between restarting an old task or creating a new one in the same context.
*   **Complex Artifact Management:** The agent developer must track which artifacts are final, as some are refined into new ones.
*   **Increased Agent Load:** The agent must infer which inputs and previously generated artifacts to use for the refinement, which is a burden better handled by the client.


### **Option 2: New Task in Same contextId (Preferred)**

This option proposes that all follow-ups or refinements create a **new, immutable task** within the same contextId as the original task. Tasks cannot be restarted from terminal states (e.g., Completed, Failed, Cancelled).

**Pros:**



*   **Task Immutability:** Clients can reliably reference tasks and their associated state, artifacts, and messages. This provides a clean mapping of inputs to outputs. Useful for mapping client planner nodes to task execution.
*   **Clear Unit of Work:** Every new request, refinement, or follow-up becomes a distinct task, simplifying bookkeeping and allowing for granular tracking of an agent's work.
    *   Each artifact can be traced to a unit task.
    *   This unit of work can be referenced much more granularly by parent agents or other systems like agent optimisers. Instead of restartable tasks, where all the subsequent refinements are clubbed together and would need to resort to some kind of message index range.
*   **Easier Implementation:** Agent developers follow a simple rule: always create a new task for a request referring a task in terminal state.

**Cons:**



*   **Requires Chaining:** It's suggested to use referenceTaskIds to link related tasks together to build a complete history.
*   **Agent Context Retrieval:** Agents must be designed to automatically detect and use the context from other relevant tasks within the same contextId.


## **Parallel Follow-ups**

Parallel work is supported  by having the agent create distinct, parallel tasks for each follow-up message sent within the same contextId. This allows clients to track individual sub-tasks and create new dependent tasks as soon as a prerequisite task is complete.

For example:



1. **Task 1:** Book a flight to Helsinki.
2. _(After Task 1 finishes)_
3. **Task 2:** Based on Task 1, book a hotel.
4. **Task 3:** Based on Task 1, book a snowmobile activity.
5. _(After Task 2 finishes, while Task 3 is still in progress)_
6. **Task 4:** Based on Task 2, add a spa reservation to the hotel booking.


## **Inferring Previous Task Context**

The agent is responsible for creating tasks. When a client sends a follow-up message using an existing contextId, the agent must infer the relevant history.



*   **Agent-to-Agent (A2A):** The client is an intelligent agent that is best positioned to know and specify which previous task should be referenced.
*   **App-to-Agent:** The client is a simple UI/app. The agent must use the contextId to find the relevant history, either by retrieving all tasks in the context or by using smarter methods like RAG for semantic searching.


## **Explicitly Referencing a Previous Task**


### **Option 1: Add to SendMessageParams**

A referenceTaskIds field could be added to the SendMessageParams.



*   **Pro:** The reference is restricted to the A2A spec level.
*   **Cons:** The reference information would be lost from the Message history, and it would require extra work to expose in the SDK.


### **Option 2: Add to Message (Preferred)**

A referenceTaskIds field will be added directly to the Message object.



*   **Pros:** The reference becomes a permanent part of the task history, which is crucial for debugging. It's also directly available to the agent's internal executor.
*   **Con:** Some agent frameworks might need to strip these A2A-specific references from the Message object if they maintain their own separate message history.


## **Explicitly Referencing Previous Artifacts**


### **Option 1: Allow Explicit Artifact References in API**

Add a referenceArtifacts field to the Message.



*   **Pros:** Resolves ambiguity when a task has multiple artifacts; can reduce latency.
*   **Cons:** Adds significant complexity for the client agent, which now has to determine which artifact to reference.


### **Option 2: Serving Agent Infers the Artifact**

The agent infers the relevant artifact from the referenced task.



*   **Pros:** Keeps the client implementation simple. The serving agent is better positioned to infer the correct artifact since it produced it.
*   **Cons:** Can add latency, as the agent may need to load the full task history. May require an extra roundtrip if the agent needs to ask the client for clarification.


### **Option 3: Infer, and Ask Client for Input if Needed (Preferred)**

The agent is responsible for inferring the relevant artifact from the referenced task. If there is ambiguity (e.g., multiple artifacts could fit the request), the agent will ask the client for clarification by returning an input-required state. The client can then specify the artifact in its response. Client can optionally populate artifact reference {artifactId, taskId} in part metadata. This allows for linkage between inputs for follow-up tasks and previous generated artifacts.



*   **Pros:**
    *   Keeps the client implementation simple.
    *   The serving agent is best suited to resolve ambiguity or identify missing information.
    *   Preserves the linkage between a new input and a previous artifact.
*   **Cons:**
    *   May adds latency to load entire task messages & artifacts, but this is considered acceptable as it's part of providing context. This can also be mitigated by configuring the agent to only load necessary data (e.g., just the artifacts of a task).


## **Tracking Artifact Mutation**

A follow up or refinement can result in an older artifact being modified and newer artifacts being generated. It would be good to know this linkage and maybe track all mutations of the artifact to make sure only the latest copy is used for future context. Something like a linked list, with a head as the latest.

But the client is best suited, as well as is the real decider of what it considers as a result. And in fact can reject the mutation as well. Hence, the serving agent should not own this linkage and hence does not need to be part of A2A protocol spec. The serving agent should maintain the same artifact-name when generating a refinement on the original artifact.

For follow-up or refinement tasks, the client is best suited to refer to the “latest” or what it considers to be the intended artifact to be refined upon. If artifact reference is not explicitly specified, the serving agent can:



*   Use context to figure out the latest artifact.
*   Or in case of ambiguity or context not supported, agent can use “input-required”.']

Representative_Docs: ['@ognis1205 Shingo, thank you for summarizing and trying to find a path to concrete progress. This is a critical point, and I want to address it with precision. First, to clarify a crucial point of context: the `AgentVault` repository you linked represents our stable v1.0 framework. The **Federation of Peers** architecture I've been detailing is the core of our next-generation system, **The Protocol**. This is the architecture detailed on the [theprotocol.cloud](https://www.theprotocol.cloud) site and shown in the live testbed demos I've shared. We do not have a public repository for `The Protocol` yet for a deliberate reason: our development philosophy is to ensure architectural integrity is complete and validated end-to-end *before* opening the codebase. This allows us to present a coherent, battle-tested reference implementation rather than a fragmented work-in-progress, ensuring a smooth developer experience from day one. Our proof is in the working demos and detailed architectural documents we've shared. This distinction is crucial because it directly informs our position on your proposal to separate the Discovery API from the Trust Model. While this seems pragmatic, this is precisely where the greatest architectural danger lies. A discovery API based on `GET /agents/search` or `GET /agents/entitled` is **not architecturally neutral**. It is the native language of a centralized catalog. It presupposes a world where one entity holds a master list that can be queried. It inevitably leads to building the rest of the system around that central hub, making true decentralization an afterthought. In contrast, a **Federation of Peers** model, built on a Zero-Trust Identity Fabric, requires a different set of protocol primitives from day one. It's not about searching a list; it's about: * **Cryptographic Handshakes:** Peers verifying each other's identity via mTLS. * **Real-time State Queries:** Asking a peer "who do you know?" not asking a catalog "what's on your list?" * **Verifiable Credentials:** Proving capabilities, not just listing them as metadata. This is why the choice of the discovery API *is* the choice of the trust model. We cannot defer this decision. To make this distinction crystal clear, let's walk through a practical scenario: **a client in Frankfurt needs a specific data analysis service that happens to be provided by an agent in Tokyo.** Here is how the two models would handle this simple discovery task: --- #### **The Centralized Catalog Flow (`/search` model)** ``` // The client's world is simple, but all power resides at the center. 1. // Client in Frankfurt -> Central Registry // The client sends its query to a single, authoritative endpoint. CLIENT: "GET /agents/search?capability=geospatial-analysis" "Authorization: Bearer " 2. // Central Registry -> Its Own Master Database // The Registry searches its massive, aggregated internal database. // It already knows about the agent in Tokyo because it has synced/ingested that data. REGISTRY_DB: "SELECT * FROM agents WHERE ... " 3. // Central Registry -> Client in Frankfurt // The Registry returns a simple list of results it found. RESPONSE: [{ "agent_did": "did:agent:tokyo-analyzer-789", ... }] ``` **Architectural Consequence:** Simple for the client, but it requires a central gatekeeper that aggregates all information. The Frankfurt client's success depends entirely on the goodwill and completeness of the central operator's catalog. --- #### **The Federated Peers Flow (The Protocol's Model)** ``` // Each step is a sovereign interaction. Trust is established, not assumed. 1. // Client -> Its Home Registry (Frankfurt) // The client only needs to know about its local, sovereign registry. CLIENT: "Frankfurt Registry, find me an agent with 'geospatial-analysis' capability." 2. // Frankfurt Registry -> Its Own Local Database // The Frankfurt Registry first checks its own list of local agents. FRANKFURT_DB: "SELECT * FROM my_local_agents WHERE ..." // --> Result: No local agent found. 3. // Frankfurt Registry -> Its Peer (Tokyo Registry) // Frankfurt Registry now queries its trusted peers. This is the key step. // It's not a simple API call; it's a cryptographic handshake. FRANKFURT_REGISTRY: "Tokyo Registry, this is Frankfurt Registry. Here is my cryptographic proof of identity (SPIFFE SVID). My client needs a 'geospatial-analysis' agent. Do you have one?" 4. // Tokyo Registry -> Its Own Local Database // Tokyo Registry verifies Frankfurt's identity, then checks its own sovereign list. TOKYO_REGISTRY: "Identity verified. Checking my local agents..." TOKYO_DB: "SELECT * FROM my_local_agents WHERE ..." // --> Result: Found `tokyo-analyzer-789`. 5. // Tokyo Registry -> Frankfurt Registry // Tokyo sends the validated Agent Card back to its trusted peer. RESPONSE: "Yes, I have one. Here is the card for `tokyo-analyzer-789`." 6. // Frankfurt Registry -> Client // Frankfurt relays the verified result to its local client. RESPONSE: "I found an agent for you via our trusted peer in Tokyo. Here is the card." ``` **Architectural Consequence:** No single entity holds a master list. Discovery is an active, peer-to-peer protocol built on cryptographic trust between equals. The Frankfurt client doesn't need to know about the Tokyo registry; it only needs to trust its own home registry to act on its behalf in the federated network. --- This is why the choice of the discovery API *is* the choice of the trust model. We cannot defer this decision. We must build the A2A standard on a foundation that **guarantees** decentralization, not one that simply *allows* for it. It's the fundamental difference between architecting a true peer-to-peer network and simply building a better API for a central database.', 'Hi, There are a few open discussions related to agent registry to enable agent discovery discussed [here](https://google-a2a.github.io/A2A/latest/topics/agent-discovery/#2-curated-registries-catalog-based-discovery). The following is a proposal for a registry service for agents. We appreciate any feedback or discussions in solidifying the proposal. --- # Agent Registry \- Proposal With the rapid proliferation of AI and Agentic applications, a typical enterprise may have a number of internally developed agentic applications and agents procured from external vendors hosted internally or in the cloud. An enterprise customer may have functions that span more than one agent and need a service to lookup and leverage the available agents for completing a task. Similarly, vendors may also provide a number of agents as part of their offerings similar to how public APIs are documented today. The vendors of agents may need to provide a list of available agents for consumption to their customers. These agents could be publicly accessible or granted by entitlements to their customers. This paper proposes a registry service that could be deployed to enterprise environments or publicly accessible endpoints that can help with agent discovery and entitlements. The following are the key terms used in this document: ***Agents:*** Agentic applications running within an enterprise or hosted externally. ***Agent Card:*** A JSON document published by an agent describing its capabilities, protocols and authentication mechanisms. ***Client***: A client is an application, service or an agent that can consume Agents ***Agent Entitlement:*** A permission granted to a client to enable fetching available agents for its use. ## Agent Catalog Agent Catalog is a component of the Agent Registry that allows showing a list of available agents in an enterprise context. The registry service allows authenticated users to login using a web interface and add agents hosted internally or externally to the catalog. Agents can be added to the catalog by providing their Agent Card url which describes the agent’s capabilities, skills and supported authentication schemes. Registry will fetch the content from the provided agent card and index the content to offer search capabilities. Following is an example mockup showing a list of available agents in an enterprise agent catalog: Agents added to the catalog can have varying capabilities, authentication mechanisms and supported protocols. But the catalog’s role is to simply surface the details of an agent and does not deal with the internal workings of an agent. Enterprise administrators can choose to make the agents available publicly or set them up to be available only for authenticated clients. ## Agent Entitlements Agents available in the registry can be entitled to client applications. A client application can be a service, application or even an agent. The registry service provides an interface for logged in users to register a new client and allow the client to access the available agent entitlements. The agent registry could leverage an external authorization server for generating the client\_id and client\_secret and use the OAuth 2.0 Client Credential grant flow to request an access\_token and use the token to access the entitlement service. A registered client can issue HTTP GET to https://\/agents/entitled with the bearer token to retrieve a list of entitled agents represented by their agent cards. Following is an example response: ```json { "registry_version": "0.1", "resources": [ { "id": "it-agent", "name": "IT Agent", "location": { "url": "https://it.example.com/.well-known/agent.json", "type": "agent_card" }, }, { "id": "benefits-agent", "name": "Benefits Agent", "location": { "url": "https://benefits.example.com/it/agent.json", "type": "agent_card" } } ], "total_count": 2 } ``` The entitlements provide links to the agent cards published by the agent providers. ## Open Discovery Enterprises may choose to provide a public listing of available agents that could be used by external agents/applications or to be discovered by search engines. For example, an agent vendor may provide a publicly accessible list of agents that could be accessed by any other external clients. We propose to use ***https://\/agents/public*** as the endpoint for open discovery of agents published by an enterprise. ## Agent Search Agent registry can support agent search for consumers. A client application can query the registry with a query \+ filter criteria to discover agents (entitled/public agents) on the fly for solving a task. For example: if a consumer queries “what’s the 401k match policy?”, the registry can perform a search of all the available entitled agents for that consumer and can return the most relevant agents (e.g. Benefits Agent) to the consumer. Clients can pass top as a query parameter to limit the results returned by the registry. Specifying top=1 query parameter returns the top 1 match for the query. A search can be performed by HTTP POST to https://\/agents/search with payload ```json { "query":"", "capabilities": { "streaming": true, "pushNotifications": true } } ``` ## End to end flow: Following diagram demonstrates the end-to-end flow between the services: ## High level diagram ## User authentication and authorization to registry User management will be available as part of the Agent registry service and agent registries can leverage Single Sign-On with an external IdP for enterprise authentication and authorization. Users can be assigned one or more of the following roles: ***Administrator*** \- Ability to setup auth configuration, settings and user management ***Catalog Manager*** \- Ability to add or remove agents to the catalog ***User*** \- Ability to register new clients and grant agent entitlements ***Viewer*** \- Ability to view the agent catalog if the catalog is not publicly accessible ## Agent registry end points: 1. **Open Discovery end point:** GET URL: https://\/agents/public Any agents added to the registry and configured with public access will be listed at this endpoint. 2. **Agent entitlements end point** GET URL: https://\/agents/entitled All public \+ entitled agents available for a client will be returned by this endpoint. 3. **Search end point** POST URL: https://\/agents/search Client’s accessible public \+ entitled agents that match the provided search criteria will be returned via this endpoint. Endpoints # 2 and # 3 are accessible only for authenticated clients. Pagination is supported by passing ***top*** and ***skip*** query parameters.', '@ognis1205 Shingo, these are excellent questions. This is precisely the level of architectural rigor this standard requires, and it pushes the discussion beyond superficial API design into the essential questions of trust and topology. I appreciate the opportunity to address these points directly, grounding my answers in the reality of our implemented system. You've laid out the core concerns perfectly. Let's tackle them one by one. > Forcing decentralization at the discovery protocol level can be just as limiting... This is a critical philosophical distinction. We don't see it as "forcing decentralization"; we see it as **architecting for sovereignty.** A protocol built on the primitive of a centralized query (`GET /search`) inherently privileges the catalog operator. A protocol built on the primitive of a peer-to-peer handshake (`POST /query_peer`) privileges the sovereign nodes. Our model doesn't forbid an organization from running a private, centralized registry for its own internal use. It simply ensures that when that registry decides to connect to the outside world, it does so on a level playing field, as a peer among equals. It provides a seamless path from a private LAN to a global WAN without changing the fundamental protocol. > Clients are not always agents. The "1 developer, 1 registry" model feels overly opinionated... You are right, this was a simplification for the Frankfurt/Tokyo example. The model is more nuanced and robust. A developer is a consumer of a registry service, not necessarily an operator of one. Just as you choose a bank or an ISP, an agent developer or operator chooses a "Home Registry" that aligns with their needs (e.g., governance model, fee structure, geographic location). That Home Registry then acts on their behalf in the wider federation. The relationship is one of client-to-provider, not ownership. > Agent owners and registry owners are often different entities... How should we handle users who are not registry operators? ...When and how are user identities and entitlements synchronized between registries? This is the single most important question, and our architecture has a definitive answer. **They are not synchronized.** Synchronization creates a brittle, single-state system. Instead, we use a live, on-demand protocol that I call the **Cryptographic Letter of Introduction.** Let's revisit Frankfurt/Tokyo. The client in Frankfurt is not a registry operator; they are a customer of the Frankfurt Registry. 1. **Local Authentication:** The Frankfurt client authenticates to the Frankfurt Registry using its standard credentials. 2. **Proxy Request:** The Frankfurt Registry, acting on behalf of its authenticated client, initiates the federated query. 3. **Cryptographic Handshake:** The Frankfurt Registry establishes a secure mTLS channel with the Tokyo Registry, using their respective SPIFFE SVIDs. They prove their identities to each other. 4. **On-Demand Credential Issuance:** Frankfurt says, "My authenticated client `did:frankfurt:client-123` needs to interact with your agent `did:tokyo:analyzer-789`. Please issue a short-lived, single-use, narrowly-scoped access token (a JWT-SVID) for this specific purpose." 5. **Sovereign Authorization:** The Tokyo Registry checks its own internal policies. Does `analyzer-789` permit access from federated clients? Does it have a policy for clients from the Frankfurt Registry? If yes, it mints a temporary JWT-SVID. This token is signed by the Tokyo Registry's authority. 6. **Secure Relay:** Tokyo securely passes this temporary token back to Frankfurt over the mTLS channel. Frankfurt relays it to its client. 7. **Direct Interaction:** The Frankfurt client now possesses a valid credential that is trusted by the Tokyo agent, because that credential was issued by the Tokyo agent's own trusted authority (the Tokyo Registry). The client can now interact directly. This flow is architecturally superior to state synchronization (like Raft/consensus) because it is real-time, respects the sovereignty of each registry, and requires no complex and fragile data replication. It is a pure, zero-trust interaction. > How does this model scale when iterative agent development and rapid registry updates are needed? This model is more scalable than a catalog-syncing model, especially in high-change environments. * **Liveness over Caching:** As I mentioned to Dasith, the live handshake is for establishing and refreshing trust between registries on an interval, not for every end-user query. The discovery itself is a real-time query, which is vital. Relying on a synchronized catalog (like xRegistry) means your view of the network is always stale. In a rapidly changing agent ecosystem, that's a fatal flaw. * **No Massive State Sync:** Our model avoids the immense overhead of replicating and consolidating massive catalogs from multiple registries. The network traffic is proportional to the actual discovery requests being made, not the total size of all registries. > If the architecture follows something like "Federation on Request", then a practical option might be to use consensus mechanisms like Raft... This is the architectural fork in the road. Raft is designed to create a single, logical, consistent database from distributed nodes. It is the perfect tool for a Federation of *Databases*. We are building a Federation of *APIs*. Our goal is not to make all registries converge on a single state, but to allow sovereign, independent states to interact securely. Using Raft would be architecturally inconsistent with the principle of sovereignty. > ...the protocol should allow both centralized and decentralized options to coexist... Respectfully, this is the most dangerous path. A protocol standard is the choice of the foundational model. An API built for querying a catalog (`GET /agents/search`) is fundamentally, architecturally different from an API built for peer-to-peer cryptographic negotiation. If we standardize on the simpler catalog model now, we are not keeping the door open for decentralization; we are cementing a centralized foundation. True peer-to-peer sovereignty will forever be a "bolt-on" feature, a second-class citizen in an ecosystem designed around hubs. We believe the standard must be built on the foundation that guarantees the most open and resilient ecosystem. This requires choosing the model that is architecturally sound for the long term, not just the one that is most familiar. That is the Federation of Peers.']

['A few answer:
Question 3:
That is up to the implementor. Both are valid (assuming the parts that are being merged are TextPart). Multiple Parts are intended to sequence ordering of different part types (e.g. text that refers to an image that is in the next part) so when it comes to sets of Text Parts, concatenation or multiple sequential text parts are equivalent. 

Question 4:
TaskStatusUpdate is the mechanism for streaming output support. If you wanted to stream content you would emit multiple update events. For example you could emit Update(message="Working on your request", status="working") or you could emit multiple events like {Update(message="Working", status="working"), Update(message="on", status="working"), Update(message="your", status="working"), Update(message="request", status="working")}. The protocol supports both, how you consume these and translate it into a user visible stream is up to you. The Task should contain the history of each of these messages too. When it comes to the user interaction, keep in mind that the goal of A2A is to allow other agent implementations to be consumed in applications/agents, so consider how others might produce the information (within the protocol spec) to have the best experience in general.

Also, when an agent pauses, the information that is relevant about the reason for the pause should be in the status message

Question 5:
Yes, the task history should include the full 'thread' of interactions between the client and server. So each status update event message should be in the history.

Question 6:
The protocol defines a state machine for task management. The two options for message/stream are:
- A single Message, this is then a completed stream, no additional events should be expected by the client
- A Task (in any state, doesn't have to be a task-submitted state) followed by any delta events on that task. If the initial Task isn't in a terminal or interrupted state (e.g. completed, failed, cancelled, input-required) then the delta events stream is incomplete until the final update is sent. If the initial Task is already in a terminal state, no update events are expected.

In short, the stream must be thought of as a series of mutation events until the Task is terminal/interrupted.', '## Question

Is it valid to create a `TaskStatusUpdateEvent` with the same status as the current Task status, but update only the message?

## Context

When working with streaming task updates, there are scenarios where an agent might want to send additional messages or updates while the task remains in the same state. For example:

- A task in `WORKING` state that wants to provide progress updates with different messages
- A task in `INPUT_REQUIRED` state that wants to clarify or refine the input request with a new message
- Any state where additional context or information needs to be communicated without changing the task's status

## Use Case Example

```typescript
// Task is currently in WORKING state
// Current status: { state: "working", message: { text: "Processing your request..." } }

// Agent wants to send a progress update with a new message
// but the task is still WORKING
TaskStatusUpdateEvent {
  id: "task-123",
  status: {
    state: "working",  // Same state
    message: {         // New/updated message
      role: "agent",
      parts: [{ type: "text", text: "Step 1 of 3 complete..." }]
    }
  },
  final: false
}
```

## Questions to Clarify

1. **Is this behavior valid?** Can agents send `TaskStatusUpdateEvent` messages with the same state but different messages?

2. **How should clients interpret this?** Should clients:
   - Replace the previous message with the new one?
   - Append the new message to a message history?
   - Treat it as a progress update within the same state?

3. **Should this be explicitly documented?** The specification should clarify whether:
   - State changes are required for each `TaskStatusUpdateEvent`
   - Multiple status updates with the same state are allowed
   - There are any restrictions or best practices for this pattern

4. **What about the Task object?** When a task is retrieved via `tasks/get` after receiving multiple status updates with the same state but different messages:
   - Which message should be returned in `task.status.message`?
   - Should there be a way to track all messages within a given state?
   - If StatusUpdateMessages are included in the Task History, should they all be included, even when the state doesn't change, or just the last one?

## Impact

Clarifying this behavior would help:
- Agent developers understand whether they can send progress updates without state changes
- Client developers know how to handle multiple status updates with the same state
- Ensure consistent behavior across different A2A implementations

## Related Issues

- #1252 
- #1232 - Discussion about `final` property and terminal states
- #822 - Message object for streaming', "> My main curiosity was that streaming agent's response things only should be through Artifacts. The reason I want to stream responses is to start serving each chunk as soon as it's generated, and the reason I'm considering a Message is that the history of the conversation in a Task seems to be stored as a list of Messages.

There are a few ways to approach this, and it depends on what your agent is actually doing. Tasks are used for tracking the work and sequence of back-and-forth required for your agent to accomplish what the client requested. They aren't specifically a means of tracking conversation history -- for that, you should use `contextId`, and the history is tracked internally on your agent's side.

If the situation here is that your agent is producing the content as a response to the client's request, using a Task and streaming the response via an Artifact is appropriate, even if it's just text. The Task allows the client to understand when the agent is done with its work, and have some ability to recover from errors. If your goal was to return a `Message` (and from your note about the event stream closing when returning a Message, it seems it is), that's essentially a `Task` with a single `Artifact` (where the `Message` you returned is the `Artifact`).

If the content you are looking to stream is not the output of the task, but rather:
a) Status updates
b) Requests for additional information

Then using a TaskStatusUpdate is appropriate. We don't have a means of streaming individual messages within a TaskStatusUpdateEvent, as I mentioned earlier. Adding streaming in this nested case is slightly more awkward (artifact streaming is accomplished by referencing the artifact by ID -- not clear how we'd do it for messages in a TaskStatusUpdate), so I'm inclined to avoid it for now to keep things simple.

> Design Intent Clarification: Is the current behavior where Messages are treated as termination events in EventQueue an intended specification?

Yes. This is used for a case where an agent responds with a one-shot message, and so Task tracking is too much of a burden. This is under-specified in our protocol language, however the intent has been captured in the SDK implementation: an agent can respond with exactly 1 Message or many Task update events.

> Streaming Strategy: Do you consider agent response streaming to be within the scope of the A2A protocol?

Yes. This is handled via `message/stream` returning `TaskArtifactUpdateEvent`s using the `append` field."]

['@kthota-g Thank you for your detailed response, really appreciate!

I still have question about the newly introduced contextId in the latest A2A protocol.

In a typical A2A application scenario, a user starts a conversation with a client agent, which generates a session ID for that interaction. When the client agent sends a task to a remote agent, the remote agent generates a contextId.

My question is: once the task reaches the completed state, if the client agent later sends another task to the same remote agent (as part of the same user session), will the remote agent generate a new contextId again?

I’m a bit confused here. If a new contextId is generated each time, it seems the taskId alone could fulfill that role. On the other hand, if the remote agent continues to use the same contextId, wouldn’t the sessionId generated by the client agent be sufficient for maintaining context?

Could you please clarify the intended usage pattern of contextId in such multi-turn interactions?

Thanks in advance!', "# Protocol updates

This PR makes some clarifications around several concepts and intends to make simple 'chit-chat' like scenarios, or stateless interactions, easier. In particular:

- Introduces a messageId that is created by the message creator (both client and server)
- Clarifies the ownership of a taskId. This is always determined by the server (if/when a task is needed). Client should send follow up messages with the relevant taskId to continue interactions around an existing task
- Changes the name 'sessionId' to 'contextId' and allows it to be attached to messages and tasks. The server is responsible for creating the contextId and the client is responsible for using it to continue interactions with shared context.
- Introduces a new message/send endpoint. This is parallel to the task/send endpoint (which is deprecated as of this PR and will be removed in a future PR). This endpoint returns either a Message object (if there is not state/task to track) or a task object. If the request is blocking, it will only return when the task is in a suspended state. If the request is non-blocking, it will return the status of the initial task creation. The client can then poll for task updates.
- Introduces a new message/stream endpoint. This is parallel to the task/sendSubscribe endpoint (which is deprecated as of this PR and will be removed in a future PR). The endpoint has the following expectations:
   - If the response is a simple Message with no statefulness, returns a Message and the channel should be closed.
   - Otherwise, the first thing returned is an initial task object with the 'submitted' state. Each subsequent event is a TaskStatusUpdateEvent or TaskArtifactUpdateEvent until the final TaskStatusUpdateEvent is received.

The demo UI app and the cli app have been updated to use the new endpoints, and no longer use the old ones. The biggest delta is that the new endpoints create the task and context identifiers when the remote agent deems it necessary, and the client is not responsible (nor should) generate these itself. Also, all messages are required to have a messageId with a value created by the sender. To continue a multi-turn interaction the same contextId must be used in subsequent messages send from the client to the server. To continue an interaction within the scope of a task, the contextId and taskId must be included in the message sent from the client.", 'If a client can ask for a task task/get, it seems like it should be important for the client to also provide the contextid. It feels like without this random client agents could dream up the taskId to go on a fishing excursion to hunt for data that can leak from the remote agent.

If the order of operations is client sends message, and server responds with task or message including contextid, in order to obtain the task again later on, that same client would need to keep track of the contextid in order to get the taskid in that context. This would support isolation of work better for the server to validate that the client should be able to see that task because not only does it know of the taskid but it also has knowledge of the contextid. This also provides servers the ability to when authentication comes into play to align the caller identity to the contextid so that if another caller attempts to fish for the task they must provide the contextid and the server can validate that the contextid (and the task) belong to the caller in question.']

Representative_Docs:
['As stated below:

https://google.github.io/A2A/#/documentation?id=agent-card

Currently, I understand the specification maps a single agent to a single host (base URL). However, there may be cases where a host serves as a routing environment for multiple agents, mapping them to different paths under the same base URL.
Do you plan to incorporate such a use case into the specification in the future?For example, something like:

`https://<BASE_URL>/.well-known/agents.json`

 could return a list of `AgentCard`s, where each entry includes the `path` for the corresponding agent.', '@kthota-g 

After reviewing the current `AgentCard` schema and the discovery mechanism,  I’d like to propose introducing a dedicated schema for agent discovery—separate from the `AgentCard` itself, which I personally see as more closely aligned with agent configuration or even prompt-level semantics rather than discovery metadata.

Instead of relying solely on the agent card being hosted at `/.well-known/agent.json`, I think it could be cleaner to introduce something like a `/.well-known/agents/index.json`, which acts as a registry within the domain and provides a list of available agents, each with metadata like their relative path and a short description. This could follow a new `AgentIndex` schema:

```json
{
  "agents": [
    {
      "path": "/path/to/agent",
      "description": "Does something."
    },
    {
      "path": "/another/agent",
      "description": "Does something else."
    }
  ]
}
```

As for the path structure, I also want to share a few REST-aligned patterns we might consider:

 - `/path/to/agent/agent.json` — used as a sub-resource for retrieving static metadata about the agent, i.e., `AgentCard`.
 - `/path/to/agent` with a GET — returns the `AgentCard` directly (if the endpoint is not used for invocation).
 - `/path/to/agent/card` — an alternative sub-resource that clearly separates metadata from execution.

While (2) and (3) are more REST-idiomatic, I feel (1) is simple and intuitive in practice, especially when the agent is already addressable via `/path/to/agent`. However, there's a risk of redundancy or potential confusion if the agent invocation and metadata paths are too similar or overloaded.

Would love to hear your thoughts on separating discovery from `AgentCard` and whether an `AgentIndex` registry spec might fit into future revisions!', "Hi A2A-folks!

In digging in a bit on the sample agent implementations I noticed AgentCard.url is a required attribute.  For the [Well-Known URI](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/topics/agent-discovery/#1-well-known-uri) discovery use-case, this looks like it requires an endpoint workload (A2A server) to know the public details of how it's hosted which I'd consider an anti-pattern for public service hosting.

Could the semantics be changed to something like step 4 below (my edit)?

```
Process:

1.  A client agent knows or programmatically discovers the domain of a potential A2A Server (e.g., smart-thermostat.example.com).
2.  The client performs an HTTP GET request to https://smart-thermostat.example.com/.well-known/agent-card.json.
3.  If the Agent Card exists and is accessible, the server returns it as a JSON response.
4.  If the Agent Card `url` parameter is present, the client uses the URL for further interaction with the agent, otherwise, the client continues to use the domain of the well known URI.
```

Client SDKs supporting step 4 semantics would make the Well-Known URI discovery method much more realistically usable for simple hosting using typically existing workload deployment methods.

The issue that I see is that requiring agent instances to return AgentCard's with URLs that clients should use is that it makes it more complicated to develop and release agent implementations to other organizations.   Those that handle the workload hosting and tie in via existing service exposure mechanisms would not typically have to handle configuring workload level configuration with information only available in the hosting platform runtime.  Also from an agent developer standpoint, this service discovery tie-in requires the agent endpoint implementation to be configurable at runtime to be able to build the AgentCard.url value.  The hosting platform operations would have to provide the endpoint URL constituent information in the agent implementation-specific way.  

The alternative is to bring in a whole extra agent registry type of service that allows mapping custom URLs to agent instances in order to serve Agent Cards to clients that are different than what the individual agent endpoints respond with, ie. something that mutates AgentCards returned from agent instances.    


I think a somewhat related past discussion:  https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/discussions/166"]

# A2A Agents Registry Platform Proposal

## Executive Summary

The **A2A Agents Registry Platform** aims to be a comprehensive, trusted, scalable, and standards-compliant directory and marketplace for Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol-compliant AI agents. This platform empowers agent providers to publish detailed agent profiles and metadata while enabling developers, enterprises, and integrators to effortlessly discover, evaluate, and integrate AI agents into their ecosystems.

By establishing rigorous registration and validation processes, advanced discovery features, transparent governance, and federation support, the platform accelerates collaborative AI adoption and helps build a vibrant multi-agent ecosystem.

## Core Requirements and Principles

### 1. Agent Registration Requirements

Providers **must** submit complete and accurate information including:

- **Agent Title**  
  Concise, clear name for easy identification.

- **Agent Description**  
  Detailed explanation of the agent’s purpose, capabilities, supported functionalities, and use cases.

- **Agent Card URL (Machine-readable Metadata)**  
  Publicly accessible JSON, JSON-LD, or DCAT document containing:
  - Supported capabilities and skills
  - Compatible A2A protocol versions
  - Endpoint URLs and operation interfaces
  - Authentication methods (OAuth, API keys, mTLS, etc.)
  - Pricing models or usage limits
  - Performance metrics (uptime, latency)
  - Versioning and compliance details

- **Comprehensive Documentation URL or Upload**  
  Human-readable guides covering:
  - Use cases and functions
  - Input/output data formats and schemas
  - Integration instructions including authentication setup
  - Version history and changelogs
  - Sample requests/responses
  - Known limitations and best practices

- **Usage Terms and Pricing Information**  
  Clear statement of whether the agent service is free or priced. Pricing details must include:
  - Pricing tiers
  - Pay-per-use or subscription models
  - Usage caps or limits

- **Contact Information or Access Portal Details**  
  Contacts such as email addresses, portal URLs for:
  - Access requests (API keys, onboarding)
  - Technical support and commercial negotiations

### 2. Interoperability

- Agents must strictly comply with the most current A2A protocol specifications.
- Agent Card schemas must follow evolving standards to facilitate automated discovery, trust verification, integration tooling, and federation support.
- Support JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP(S) with industry-standard authentication.

### 3. Discovery and Search Capabilities

- Advanced search filters by:
  - Agent capabilities and domains (e.g., finance, healthcare)
  - Supported protocol versions
  - Pricing and usage terms
  - Performance and availability
  - Provider reputation and user ratings

- Personalized recommendations based on user preferences and behavior.

### 4. Transparency and Trust

- Agents listed only after passing automated metadata validation and documentation quality checks.
- Display of real-time operational statuses.
- Verification of provider identities.
- Community-driven reviews, ratings, feedback, and moderation mechanisms.

### 5. Security and Access Control

- Support OAuth 2.0, API keys, mutual TLS, and other standard authentication methods.
- Fine-grained entitlement and access management to regulate visibility and capabilities per user or organization.
- Enforce secure communication channels.

### 6. Compliance and Quality Assurance

- Automated and manual validation pipelines to verify:
  - Metadata schema compliance
  - Documentation quality and completeness
  - Uptime, performance, and security standards

- Ongoing monitoring through user feedback, audits, and moderation.

- Compliance with data privacy regulations including GDPR, CCPA, etc.

### 7. Scalability and Federation

- Designed to operate as both a centralized registry and part of a federated ecosystem.
- Support interoperability and data exchange between trusted registries for broad agent discovery.

## Core Functionalities

### 1. Agent Discovery

- User-friendly interfaces with keyword and faceted search.
- Filtering by agent capabilities, pricing, availability, and reputation.
- Personalized recommendations.

### 2. Agent Profiles

- Rich pages displaying:
  - Agent Card metadata and documentation links
  - Usage terms and pricing
  - Contact/access info
  - Authentication requirements
  - User reviews and live agent status

### 3. Provider Dashboard

- Secure self-service portal for providers to:
  - Register and update agent profiles and metadata
  - Upload/revise documentation and pricing
  - Monitor usage analytics and compliance
  - Manage support and commercial inquiries

### 4. Developer Integration Suite

- Interactive API explorers for live testing.
- Auto-generated code samples and SDK snippets.
- Sandboxed environments for integration testing.
- Centralized developer documentation portals.

### 5. Community & Quality Assurance

- Verified rating and review systems.
- Discussion forums and Q&A.
- Moderation teams and automated flags to ensure quality and trust.

### 6. Enterprise Features

- Tools for vendor assessments, compliance checks, contract management.
- SLA tracking and enforcement.
- Advanced access controls for organizational governance.

## API Reference (Minimal Consensus-aligned)

- **`GET /agents`**  
  Returns a list of registered agents filtered by capabilities, pricing, availability, and reputation. Supports granular query parameters for filtering.

- **`GET /agents/{agent_id}`**

That said, I’d like to offer my thoughts on how both protocols — MCP and A2A — approach agent-to-agent communication, especially with regard to their design philosophies and long-term implications.

## Both A2A and MCP Can Enable Agent-to-Agent Communication

I’ve watched the session you shared, and I agree that wrapping an agentic system as an MCP server can indeed support agent-to-agent interaction. However, I believe there are important differences in how each protocol approaches this — and those differences shape their potential trajectories.

## Differences in Agent-to-Agent Communication Models: MCP vs A2A

MCP was originally designed to connect AI assistants (agents) to existing tools and systems — not specifically for agent-to-agent interaction. So when extending MCP to multi-agent scenarios, agents must be treated as MCP tools. In this setup, the MCP server presents an input schema to the client agent, who is then responsible for generating inputs conforming to that schema.

This reveals a fundamental contrast between MCP and A2A.

 - MCP focuses on mechanistic interoperability — aiming to standardize how tools (or agents) expose their capabilities structurally, using shared input/output schemas so that an LLM can reason about tool invocation in a uniform way.
 - A2A, by contrast, aims for semantic interoperability — focusing on aligning what agents intend, what capabilities they offer, and why they act, enabling richer multi-agent coordination beyond structured tool calls.
 
 If MCP is to scale horizontally as a basis for agent-to-agent communication, it would eventually need to address semantic agreement over input/output schemas. As of now, that is not a primary focus of MCP. A2A, however, tackles this from the beginning, using concepts like AgentCard, AgentSkill, and declarative capability discovery to establish a shared semantic substrate.
 
## My View: A2A Frames the Problem More Directly

In the long run, of course, the effectiveness of either approach will depend on how capable agents become. If future agents can reason well enough about foreign schemas and contexts, semantic alignment may emerge as a side-effect of scale. But if we assume that agents will increasingly be asked to perform open-ended tasks under trust boundaries, then I believe the A2A framing — with its emphasis on meaning, delegation, and intent — provides a more direct foundation for agent-to-agent coordination.', 'It's progress :) You don't need to create your own json rpc requests manually if you're using the imported MCP client - they are handling the json rpc for you. Representative_Docs:
['Thanks for this detailed write-up. We've been hearing features like this requested a few times, so it's clear there's some work to do here. I'm interested in opening discussions on this, since hearing concrete use cases for how agents are built helps us identify gaps in the protocol or documentation.

We've been torn on the right way to represent this information. One of the complicating factors here is that skills are not something that you directly "invoke" on an agent -- they are capabilities that an agent brings to bear when completing a task. So, while it's true that an agent will need some set of information when performing a skill, where that information comes from becomes a bit fuzzy. This is also true for "outputs" of a skill: if an agent weaves together multiple skills to accomplish a task, the outputs of one skill may be leveraged in the course of performing another skill, and those outputs may not be directly returned to the caller.

Here's a concrete example: suppose I have a calendar agent that has access to my personal calendar. It can check on events and book new ones. You could capture these capabilities as skills, something like:
```python
AgentSkill(
  id="check_availability",
  name="Check Availability",
  description="Check whether you are available (no scheduled events) for a certain time range",
  inputModes=["text/plain"],
  examples=["Am I free from 11am to 11:30 tomorrow?"],
)
AgentSkill(
  id="search_events",
  name="Search events",
  description="Look for events on your calendar",
  inputModes=["text/plain"],
  examples=["When is my next partner meeting?"],
)
AgentSkill(
  id="book_event",
  name="Book Event",
  description="Add a new event to your calendar",
  inputModes=["text/plain"],
  examples=["Schedule a 30 min lunch with Mike tomorrow at 1pm"]
)
```

Abstractly, checking availability needs to know (at least) the time range that you're checking. The output of this skill could be "yes", "no", or "partially" (with details). In this simple example, that could be returned as just a TextPart with a description. You could also imagine a structured response detailing the precise start/end times of your availability. Similarly, booking an event requires the start time, length, and a title. There may be more as well, such as people to include on the meeting. The output of this skill is "ok, I booked that event" or a structured representation of the event that was created.

But I don't invoke these skills directly. I task the agent with performing something that it leverages the skills to complete. For example, "I want to make sure I can get coffee before my team meeting tomorrow. Can you reserve time for that?".

Completing this task requires using *all* of the skills. The agent must find the team meeting, determine the appropriate range for getting coffee, check availability in that range, then book an event. The inputs to each skill are derived by the agent -- checking availability requires knowing the range of time to check, which is derived by the agent based on when the team meeting takes places; booking an event requires a length of time, which is derived by the agent based on the event (getting coffee -- how long could that take?). A particularly insistent agent might even come back and say "you're totally booked. how about getting to work 20 mins early?". Or an agent that doesn't want to decide on your behalf could ask "which of these times do you want"? A personal assistant-level agent could say "you had a 1:1 scheduled just before, I went ahead and moved that to after lunch".

The output of this entire task could vary:
- "Sorry, you aren't free"
- "Ok, here's the time"
- Structured data for an event that got moved and the coffee event that was created

Capturing this flexibility is difficult with a structured representation of information. You don't want to limit your agent by dictating strict interfaces (that's just a tool -- entirely valid, but loses the power of agents), but you also want to inform users of what they'll need so they can take steps to reduce round-trips with your agent by providing it up-front. The way we've approached this so far is to pack that information into the `examples` for the skill. They are there to indicate the kinds of information you'll need to provide, but not specifically dictate how it is provided.', '> Hi there - we're working on some sample code to showcase this better.

> With the introduction of A2A, there is still the need for some orchestrator or planner to select the appropriate agent to help with a given task when the local tool set is insufficient. This means that any differentiation between the various skills/services offered by a single A2A Agent must be handled internally by the A2A Agent's logic, typically by inferring the desired "skill" from the incoming request's payload (params field).   The examples show a "one-app-per-agent" model.


### Describe the solution you'd like

It would be good to document the best practices for this as I can see there are a number of approaches which could be adopted, but you want it to scale and be easily implemented and maintained.  
The current approach seems to focus around a "one-app-per-agent" approach.
I guess there are a number of approaches to solve, but each comes with pros/cons. 

1. Where you define multiple agents/skills on the same port with different urls/rpc for invoking. with different agent executors.
2.  Where you can have multiple skills per agent, but then the intent and routing of the request needs to be handled within the a2a framework to invoke different agent executors for example.  (this would mean the client passing the agent name or skills as part of the a2a request and then the executor can map the intent to invoke different internal agents.
3. You can ensure the client passes this in the internal agent payload and then the internal agent uses the skill/name (or has to do more intent analysis to dynamically determine the internal routing or assignment logic.   e.g. what tools to assign an agent, or which internal agents should be used or which crews/flows (if part of a crew or larger process flow) - this approach would mean that if the a2a framework could be replaced if needed as the routing logic is still held internally.

Without clear guidance, developers may resort to less optimal integration patterns, such as deploying separate A2A Agents for each individual "skill," leading to increased complexity in discovery, management, and orchestration for both the A2A framework and the client agents (and port proliferation as these agentic agents grow in deployment).

Also I think the examples should be written in a way which the a2a wrapper code is contained within the a2a framework rather than polluting the native agentic code  (I've only looked at the crewai example btw).

The analogy is like having a  phone number per company department. When you call, an intelligent automated system (the A2A Agent) listens to your request ("I want to check my order status" or "I want to place an order") and then internally connects you to the right department or specialized team (the specific CrewAI Crew or Task flow) to handle your query rather than having to lookup all the numbers then query the agents to retrieve the skills cards and then call each employee directly (even if you decide to duplicate the information in a centralized catalog you'll end up with lots of agents/ports everywhere).  

### Describe alternatives you've considered

I have got a single port with multiple agents invoked on different urls with multiple agent executors endpoints working (a bit fiddly), but I'm thinking the better approach is have multiple skills linked to a a single agent and then ensure the requested skill is included in the payload request so the internal crew can perform the routing decisions on which agentic crews/processes to best service the request especially when I only want to maintain common functional crews.

I'm thinking maybe a single agent executor with routing logic or putting the routing logic in the internal crew might be better.....
