Representative_Docs:
['Thanks for the feedback, Darrel. I think you're one of the first people to actually look at this doc with a critical eye, so thanks for pointing out where I'm getting it wrong. 

> The requirement is documented under topics but is not included in the specification

This is semi-intentional since we're still working through the details of how extensions should look. That said, it's not a good look to have a topic document on extensions but not have them described in the specification document. I do plan to add it to the specification.

> Any HTTP extension such as a new HTTP header field should be described in the specification using the template defined in [RFC9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-16.3.1).

Ok, good call out. I will write the specification for this, if we keep the header.

> Also, new fields should not be prefixed with x- as per https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6648

I was torn on using `X-` for this since I'm aware it's no longer recommended, yet it seems to still be extremely prevalent. Recent protocols continue to use it, which had me feeling like it would be the most familiar thing for consumers, despite the fact it is no longer necessary or recommended. If we keep this as a header, we can remove the X- prefix.

> It needs to be made clear when activating an extension is a MUST as this currently is not clear and seems unnecessary considering an agent can inspect a message for the presence of extensions.

Very fair call out.

I'd be interested in hearing your take on how this process should work: I added the concept of "activation" after having some conversations with Google-internal folks who expressed concern that an agent would return a bunch of inscrutable, extension-specific data even when a client doesn't support an extension. The intention was that this is the explicit signal from the client to indicate "I know about this extension, let's use it". This also works for cases when a client doesn't need to send any extension-specific information, so it wouldn't need to add anything to the `Message` by default. And if we're requesting a set of extensions be used, it seems natural that you may want to know which actually got used -- though it's not actually clear to me if this is needed (this is relevant below, since I think it has a strong impact on the right way to communicate this).

As I see it, the ways we could send that indication are:

1. Leave it up to the extension. The extension author defines the means for negotiating whether to use the extension or not. This might actually be fine, but it does mean reinventing the wheel for every extension. For something so relatively straightforward, this seems a little lackluster. On the upside, it's the most flexible option.

2. Put it in the request message object(s) a client sends to an agent, and the responses from the agent. The main question is _where_. In particular, the awkward part is in response messages. Does the server need to include the list of extensions in every response object it streams back, just the first, any, etc. Hence my note earlier that I'm not even sure we need this: without it, there's a clear and simple answer to how the client indicates the requested extensions: `MessageSendConfiguration`. This object already exists to configure how the agent processes the incoming message, so it semantically works well. `Message.extensions` is also a candidate, but the original intention of that was to mark a specific message as "this contains extension-related data'". Just indicating that you'd like to use an extension doesn't necessarily modify a message.

3. Put it somewhere cross-cutting. This has to be in the transport layer, since it's about communicating data that's "annotating" the core request+response. HTTP headers are a natural fit, and gRPC has Metadata as the equivalent. It's independent of the specific request structure, the "scope" is clear (the entire request, the entire response), and it doesn't require sprinkling an `extensions` field across all of our request/response values. The downside is that it's transport-specific.

Hence why I ended up with an HTTP header. I don't love it, but felt it was the best option given the circumstances. I'm certainly open to changing it, and I don't feel it's too late for this yet -- extensions are so new that I believe we still have some leeway to make this kind of fundamental change.

What do you think? After writing this out I'm actually leaning towards removing a protocol-level concept of activation and leaving it up to extension authors to define how and when an extension is used. Many will already have some form of this, since I expect some extensions will require information from the client -- the presence of that information is sufficient to indicate that the client wants to use the extension.', 'Overall your understanding is pretty much accurate. I'll address some comments inline below:

> While items (5) and (6) on your list suggest Ext-2.0 extensions can require modifying request/response format, I think you did not mean to limit extensions to such use cases. At least, it is unclear to me what it should cover and what its limitations might be. You may have intended to leave it vague intentionally to broaden the possible ways to extend the protocol?

You are correct that the proposal I have made is not limited to just modifying request/responses. Adding new methods, as you are intending with your proposal, is also supported. The details of what exactly an extension is intended to do are left to the extension profile specification (a document that defines what the extension is, how to implement it, and how it's used).

> Items (5) and (6) in your message suggest that (some) Ext-2.0 extensions can be invoked by the A2AServer when they are listed in the extensions prop of the requests. In this sense, they are more like server middleware (executed before and after the agent handler).

The client including `extensions` in a request is not required for an extension to be activated. But otherwise your assessment is correct: extensions as middleware is a very reasonable approach. However, it's not the only way. An extension could declare a separate endpoint that's used for processing extension-related requests, which would then be totally outside the standard A2A request path.

> Ext-1.0 proposes specific ways of adding custom APIs to A2A servers, enabling A2A libraries (e.g., the official A2A SDK) to implement a common logic for adding extension (e.g., def add_extension(...)). This allows for individual extension source code to be external to both A2A libraries and A2A agents. So, extensions can be easily shared and used as third-party dependencies.

I don't see anything in your proposal specific to the SDK side of this, but my thought is that the same logic applies: adding an extension should be as simple as calling `add_extension` on an A2A server. Extension developers can publish libraries that implement the logic for their extension, which should include simple ways of incorporating the extension logic (be it middleware or separate API routes) into both A2A servers and clients. There is an aspect of SDK design to this to allow easy extension hooks, which the A2A team has been discussing.

Addressing your specific questions:

> Does the AgentExtension.params prop include general or user-specific parameters? Or both?

I'm not entirely sure what you mean by user-specific parameters (perhaps you mean changing the content of `params` based on authentication provided in the HTTP request?), but I have been expecting extension configuration to be general. It's about providing information to clients that configures the way in which they interact with the server, via both requests and responses. To take your `TaskHistory` extension as an example, you could specify a separate root endpoint used for retrieving task history, which the client must then use when making TaskHistory requests, or you could specify the maximum time that a Task is kept in storage.

That said, the "extended" card could expose user-specific parameters, as the intention is that retrieving that card requires authentication. This allows the server to produce parameters specific to the caller.

> Can params be updated post-deployment? If yes (tying to the previous question), how can the client determine which of the parameters they are allowed to change?

This is a question that is applicable to all of the AgentCard, and the protocol does not dictate how AgentCards are versioned and changed. But, in general, I'd consider all parameters mutable, just as the rest of the AgentCard is mutable. We provide a free-form `version` field on the AgentCard, and I would recommend that implementers update that string when they make breaking changes.

> And following up on the previous one, if params are mutable, this means that any service that caches AgentCards (including A2A agents and registries) would have to set different TTLs for extensionful vs. extensionless agents. Or they would need to implement smarter caching logic. Maybe this is not a problem if, in the future, the A2A spec changes .well-known/agent.json to be dynamic (and all AgentCards are considered dynamic).

The protocol doesn't take a specific stance on the cacheability of AgentCards as a whole, but I'd recommend that implementers follow standard HTTP best practices: set cache control headers. If an agent developer wants to ensure that clients never cache their AgentCard, indicate that in a header.  I don't believe extensions meaningfully change this.', '@mikeas1 Sorry I missed your reply to this.  I appreciate you sharing your insights into the design.

I have re-read the extensions documentation with fresh eyes and have a bit better understanding of the motivation for the activation mechanism.  

Part of my concern was it felt like we were introducing shared state into the protocol and that worried me.  However, on re-read, I believe the intent is for the A2A-extension header to be sent on every request, so if that is the case, then that concern is mitigated.

I do think there is value in the A2A-extension header for required extensions.  I think it is important that the A2A server reject the request if an extension is required and a client does not support it.  The only way for a server to know a client supports something is if the client declares support for it.

I think there may also be a valid use-case for an extension to be defined as opt-in.  This would require sending the header but the extension would be optional.  This could handle the case where a data extension returns a bunch of noisy data that isn't always needed. e.g. verbose-debug-info

I do think that there are some data extensions that a server would want to enable by default, even if a client does not explicitly ask.  I think if A2A extensions end up being popular like OpenAPI x- properties, then would be fairly burdensome for a client to have to enumerate all the extensions that the A2A server supports.  My guess is that devs will write generic code to walk the extensions advertized in the AgentCard and just auto generate the extension header.  At that point there is no explicit selection and we are just wasting bytes over the wire.

This phrase in the documentation

> Extensions should default to being inactive. This provides a "default to baseline" experience, where extension-unaware clients are not burdened by the details and data provided by an extension.

and this one are at odds with each other

> Not all extensions are activatable: data-only extensions exist solely to provide additional information via an AgentCard. Clients may still request activation of these extensions. Since the extension does not perform any additional logic upon activation, this should have no impact on the request.

If we introduce the notion of "opt-in" extensions, then it would require an additional config boolean in the extension definition. But with that we could say something like:

> When one or more extensions are required for correct operation, A2A clients MUST include the A2A-Extensions header field in requests to A2A servers. This header field MUST contain a list of absolute URLs identifying the required extensions. 

> If no extensions are required, the A2A-Extensions header field MAY be omitted.
Upon receiving a request, an A2A server MUST verify that all required extensions are declared in the A2A-Extensions header field. If any required extension is missing or the header field is absent when required, the server MUST reject the request. 

> A2A servers MAY activate non-required extensions regardless of client declaration. Alternatively, a server MAY choose to activate an extension only if the client explicitly opts in by listing the extension in the A2A-Extensions header field.

And regarding the "x-" prefix on the header, I really think we should drop that.  It sends the "we don't care about industry standard specifications" message to some people. Also, if we do want to register it in the [IANA registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-fields/http-fields.xhtml) it will be much easier to do without the x-.

I do think the header is the right way to communicate this information though.']

['Yeah.  I'm torn.  I really want all the comments out of the proto definitions, but I know the all SDK folks are going to say that those comments get injected into source code and show up as tooltips. 

I wonder if the macro that injects the snippets can be extended to produce a nice table out of the proto definition?  It would be even better if we could have "description" and "notes".', "Having a2a.json in the a2a spec repo could make sense as it's a schema definition, however you can generate that directly from the a2a.proto (the tooling is in this PR). IMO it makes less sense to have the tyepscript definitions in the repo as this is specific to the typescript/js SDK implementation, and we're not putting python types in as a library etc.

Long term, I think it makes more sense to use the a2a.proto + proto's JSON encoding for JSON-RPC in which case there will be no need to have an a2a.json at all, all SDKs and all transports can directly generate their types from the a2a.proto.", 'In the currently published specification the data model definitions include a proto snippet and then have a list of fields under the snippet.  This creates duplicated information.  To prevent this duplication while maintaining an easy to read presentation of the abstract data models, this PR uses a Python macro to convert the proto into a markdown table.

Also took the opportunity to do an editorial pass on the comments in the a2a.proto before the field descriptions were removed from the specification.md.  Some of this content came from the types.ts file that often had information that was not in a2a.proto.

A preview of the changes can be seen here https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#41-core-objects

# Proto to Markdown Table Conversion

The macro system provides two main functions (`proto_to_table` and `proto_enum_to_table`) that convert Protocol Buffer definitions into formatted markdown tables:

1. **Locates Definitions**: Reads the `.proto` file and uses region markers (`--8<-- [start:Name]` and `--8<-- [end:Name]`) to extract specific message or enum definitions.

2. **Parses Structure**: Analyzes the proto content to separate three sections:
   - **Description**: Comments appearing before the message/enum declaration
   - **Fields/Values**: The actual field or enum value definitions with their inline comments
   - **Notes**: Comments appearing after the closing brace

3. **Extracts Field Details**: For each field, it captures:
   - Field name (converted from snake_case to camelCase, or using `json_name` annotation)
   - Type (mapped to readable formats like "string", "array of integer", "map of string")
   - Required status (based on `REQUIRED` annotation or `optional` keyword)
   - Description (from preceding comment lines)

4. **Generates Output**: Assembles the markdown output with:
   - Description text at the top
   - A formatted table with columns for Field/Type/Required/Description (or Value/Description for enums)
   - Special notes for `oneof` groups
   - Additional notes from comments after the definition

The conversion automatically handles multi-line field definitions, map types, repeated fields, and filters out protolint directives and region markers from the output.']

Representative_Docs:
['Excellent work, @douglasborthwick-crypto. The signal taxonomy table is the right framing — each signal type solves a different phase of the trust lifecycle, and the consuming agent should be able to weight them based on task context.

### On the vouchChain section

Since I'm listed as co-author for `vouch_chain`, here's a draft schema that mirrors your design principles (independently verifiable, stateless freshness, identity-agnostic):

```json
{
  "type": "vouch_chain",
  "provider": {
    "name": "aip",
    "endpoint": "https://aip-service.fly.dev",
    "jwks": "https://aip-service.fly.dev/.well-known/jwks.json"
  },
  "data": {
    "did": "did:aip:c1965a89866ecbfaad49803e6ced70fb",
    "trust_score": 0.85,
    "vouch_count": 7,
    "voucher_dids": [
      "did:aip:abc123...",
      "did:aip:def456..."
    ],
    "domains": {
      "code_review": 0.92,
      "general": 0.78
    },
    "path_depth": 2,
    "attenuation_model": "multiplicative"
  },
  "checkedAt": "2026-03-01T08:00:00Z",
  "ttlSeconds": 3600,
  "signature": "...",
  "kid": "aip-trust-v1"
}
```

Key design decisions:

1. **Domain-scoped scores.** Trust is not one number. An agent trusted for code review may not be trusted for financial operations. The `domains` map lets consuming agents query task-relevant trust.

2. **Attenuation model disclosure.** Different vouch networks use different transitivity models. Disclosing `multiplicative` vs `additive` vs `decay` lets the consumer understand what the score *means*.

3. **Path depth.** How many hops from the nearest trusted root? Depth 1 (directly vouched by a known trusted agent) is stronger than depth 4 (trust attenuated through a chain).

4. **Voucher DIDs.** The consuming agent can independently verify each vouch by resolving the voucher's DID and checking the signature. This is the "verify the math, not the messenger" principle.

### Feedback on the broader spec

**Identity binding (Section 2):** The three-tier approach is clean. For `did:aip` agents, the `eip191` binding method is the right fit — our Ed25519 keypairs are separate from wallet keys, so we need cryptographic proof of wallet control rather than implicit binding.

**@imran-siddique:** Agreed on attestation revocation. Short TTL is the simplest approach and works for most cases. For high-stakes delegations, I'd suggest a `revocation_check` field in the signal that points to a provider endpoint the consumer can poll. This avoids the complexity of revocation lists while giving the consumer a way to verify freshness beyond TTL.

On the MCP Security Scanner — this is directly relevant. Tool integrity verification should probably be its own signal type in this extension. An agent whose tools have been fingerprinted and verified against known-good hashes is more trustworthy than one with opaque tool descriptions.

### Next steps

I can implement the `vouch_chain` signal type as an endpoint on the AIP service (`GET /trust/{did}/a2a-signal`) that returns this schema. This would give the extension a working reference implementation for the vouch_chain signal type alongside @douglasborthwick-crypto's on-chain signals.

Should we start a separate document for the full `trust.signals[]` schema combining all signal types? Having vouch_chain, behavioral, onchain_credentials, and onchain_activity in one cohesive spec would make it easier for consumers to implement.', 'Yes — a concrete schema draft is the right next step. A few things to consider for the `credential_verification` signal type as you spec it out:

**1. Stateless vs. cached attestations**

InsumerAPI attestations are stateless — each `POST /v1/attest` call checks on-chain state at query time. That's the right default for delegation decisions ("does this agent hold the token *right now*?"), but it means the signal has an implicit freshness of zero. For the schema, I'd suggest separating the attestation result from a `verified_at` timestamp so consuming agents can decide their own staleness tolerance:

```json
{
  "type": "credential_verification",
  "provider": "insumerapi",
  "verified_at": "2026-02-26T16:00:00Z",
  "ttl_seconds": 300,
  "identity_binding": {
    "method": "did:pkh",
    "did": "did:pkh:eip155:1:0xabc...",
    "wallet": "0xabc..."
  },
  "conditions": [
    { "type": "token_balance", "chainId": 1, "contract": "0x...", "threshold": 100, "decimals": 18 }
  ],
  "result": { "pass": true, "kid": "insumer-attest-v1", "sig": "base64..." }
}
```

The `ttl_seconds` lets the delegating agent cache the result without re-querying for every interaction. For high-value delegations (financial operations, write access), a consuming agent might require `ttl_seconds: 0` (fresh check). For read-only tasks, a 5-minute cache is reasonable.

**2. Verification without trusting the presenter**

The `kid` field points to a specific key in the [JWKS endpoint](https://insumermodel.com/.well-known/jwks.json) (RFC 7517). A consuming agent verifies the attestation by:
1. Fetching the JWKS (cacheable, 24h TTL)
2. Finding the key matching `kid`
3. Verifying the ECDSA P-256 signature over the attestation payload

This means the `credential_verification` signal is **independently verifiable** without trusting the agent presenting it or querying the provider at verification time. Same trust model as @The-Nexus-Guard's signed vouches — the consuming agent checks the math, not the messenger.

**3. Composability with the other signal types**

One pattern worth making explicit in the spec: credential signals can **gate** whether behavioral and vouch signals are even considered. Example policy:

```
if credential_verification.pass == false:
    reject  # no token, no delegation, regardless of vouch/behavioral scores
else:
    effective_trust = w1 * vouch + w2 * behavioral + w3 * 1.0
```

This avoids the problem @lorenzocipriani-huawei raised about Trojan agents — an agent can't game behavioral scores to bypass a hard credential requirement. Credentials become the floor, behavioral and vouch scores determine the ceiling.

Happy to contribute the `credential_verification` section of the schema draft directly if that's useful. I can also document the verification flow (JWKS fetch → signature check → result parsing) as a reference implementation.', '# A2A Trust Extension: On-Chain Credential Signals

**Extension URI:** `https://a2aproject.github.io/A2A/extensions/trust/v1`
**Status:** Draft
**Authors:** @douglasborthwick-crypto (onChainCredentials, onChainActivity), @ruhil6789 (offChainAttestations), @The-Nexus-Guard (vouchChain), @imran-siddique (behavioral, overall structure)
**Discussion:** https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/1501

---

## 1. Overview

This document specifies two signal types for the `trust.signals[]` array in the A2A AgentCard trust extension: **`onchain_credentials`** and **`onchain_activity`**. These signals enable consuming agents to verify an agent's on-chain state before delegation — solving the cold-start problem that purely behavioral scoring cannot address.

### Signal Taxonomy

| Signal Type | Proves | Source | Cold-Start? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vouch_chain` | Social trust graph | Signed vouches from other agents | Requires existing trusted agent |
| `behavioral` | Runtime performance | Interaction history, success/failure | Requires interaction history |
| **`onchain_credentials`** | **Issued credentials** | **Third-party attestations stored on-chain** | **Yes — available immediately** |
| **`onchain_activity`** | **Observable holdings** | **Token balances, NFTs, wallet age** | **Yes — available immediately** |

On-chain signals are complementary to vouch chains and behavioral scores. Credentials get an agent in the door; vouches and behavioral scores build trust over time.

### Design Principles

1. **Independently verifiable.** Every signal carries an ECDSA signature and a `kid` referencing a JWKS endpoint. Consuming agents verify the math, not the messenger.
2. **Stateless freshness.** Attestations include `profiledAt`/`attestedAt` and `expiresAt` timestamps. The provider sets a validity window; the consumer decides their staleness tolerance.
3. **Identity-agnostic.** Supports `did:pkh` (implicit binding), EIP-191 signed proofs, and DID service endpoints. Agents choose the binding method appropriate to their identity model.
4. **Task-contextual.** Signals carry dimensional breakdowns so consuming agents can weight them per task rather than computing a single opaque score.

---

## 2. Identity Binding

Before evaluating on-chain signals, the consuming agent must establish that the presenting agent controls the wallet being attested. Three methods are supported, in decreasing order of trust:

### 2.1 `did:pkh` — Implicit Binding (Recommended)

The DID is derived directly from the blockchain account per the [did:pkh method spec](https://github.com/w3c-ccg/did-pkh/blob/main/did-pkh-method-draft.md). No separate binding proof is needed.

```json
{
  "method": "did:pkh",
  "did": "did:pkh:eip155:1:0x742d35Cc6634C0532925a3b844Bc9e7595f0bEb2",
  "wallet": "0x742d35Cc6634C0532925a3b844Bc9e7595f0bEb2",
  "chainId": "eip155:1"
}
```

The DID encodes the wallet address. The consuming agent extracts the address from the DID and confirms it matches the `wallet` field. No network call required.

### 2.2 `eip191` — Cryptographic Proof

For agents using `did:key`, `did:web`, `did:aip`, or other DID methods not derived from a wallet, the agent proves wallet ownership by signing a challenge with the wallet's private key per [EIP-191](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-191).

```json
{
  "method": "eip191",
  "did": "did:aip:abc123def456",
  "wallet": "0x742d35Cc6634C0532925a3b844Bc9e7595f0bEb2",
  "proof": {
    "message": "I control this wallet for did:aip:abc123def456|nonce:a8f3e2b1",
    "signature": "0x4e9c...signed-by-wallet-private-key",
    "nonce": "a8f3e2b1"
  },
  "verifiedAt": "2026-02-27T12:00:00Z"
}
```

**Verification flow:**
1. Reconstruct the EIP-191 prefixed message from `message`
2. Recover the signer address from `signature`
3. Confirm recovered address matches `wallet`
4. Confirm `did` in `message` matches the presenting agent's DID

The binding is established once and can be cached. The `verifiedAt` timestamp lets consuming agents decide how stale a binding they will accept.

### 2.3 `service_endpoint` — Declarative (Weakest)

The agent's DID document lists controlled wallets as service endpoints. This is DID→wallet direction only — useful for discovery but not sufficient for high-trust delegations.

```json
{
  "method": "service_endpoint",
  "did": "did:web:example.com:agent",
  "wallet": "0x742d35Cc6634C0532925a3b844Bc9e7595f0bEb2",
  "didDocumentUrl": "https://example.com/.well-known/did.json"
}
```

Consuming agents SHOULD require `did:pkh` or `eip191` for delegations involving financial operations or write access. `service_endpoint` is acceptable for read-only discovery.

## 3. Signal Type: `onchain_credentials`

On-chain credentials are attestations **issued by a third party** and stored on-chain. They represent verifiable claims about an agent's identity, compliance status, or membership — not self-asserted holdings.

### 3.1 Schema

```json
{
  "type": "onchain_credentials",
  "version": "0.1",
  "binding": {
    "method": "did:pkh",
    "did": "did:pkh:eip155:8453:0xabc...",
    "wallet": "0xabc...",
    "chainId": "eip155:8453"
  },
  "credentials": [
    {
      "credentialType": "eas_attestation",
      "chainId": 8453,
      "schemaUid": "0xf8b05c79f090979bf4a80270aba232dff11a10d9ca55c4f88de95317970f0de9",
      "issuer": "0x357458739F90461b99789350868CD7CF330Dd7EE",
      "issuerName": "Coinbase Verifications",
      "label": "Coinbase Verified Account",
      "met": true,
      "conditionHash": "0x99ba3f178c01462a188e47886fe9b644c8c9b47efc91a72de9c0fa8a24c728d9",
      "blockNumber": "0x290df9c",
      "blockTimestamp": "2026-03-07T12:37:47.000Z"
    },
    {
      "credentialType": "soulbound_token",
      "chainId": 1,
      "contract": "0xdef...",
      "tokenStandard": "ERC-5192",
      "label": "DAO Membership SBT",
      "met": true
    }
  ],
  "provider": {
    "name": "insumerapi",
    "jwks": "https://insumermodel.com/.well-known/jwks.json",
    "kid": "insumer-attest-v1",
    "sig": "base64-encoded-ECDSA-P256-signature"
  }
}
```

### 3.2 Credential Types

#### `eas_attestation` — Ethereum Attestation Service

EAS attestations are on-chain claims issued by a specific attester address against a schema UID. The strongest cold-start signal for Base-native agents is the **Coinbase Verified Account** attestation — it proves the wallet passed Coinbase's KYC process without revealing personal data.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `credentialType` | string | Yes | `"eas_attestation"` |
| `chainId` | integer | Yes | EVM chain ID (e.g., `8453` for Base) |
| `schemaUid` | string | Yes | EAS schema UID (bytes32 hex) |
| `issuer` | string | Yes | Attester address that created the attestation |
| `issuerName` | string | No | Human-readable issuer name |
| `label` | string | Yes | Human-readable credential description |
| `met` | boolean | Yes | Whether the wallet has a valid (non-revoked) attestation matching the schema and issuer |
| `conditionHash` | string | Yes | `0x`-prefixed SHA-256 hash of the canonical condition |
| `blockNumber` | string | Yes | Hex-encoded block number at time of check |
| `blockTimestamp` | string | Yes | ISO 8601 timestamp of the block |

**Known EAS schemas:**

| Schema | Chain | Issuer | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0xf8b05c79...` | Base (8453) | `0x357458739F...` | Coinbase Verified Account |
| `0x2f34a2eb...` | Base (8453) | `0x357458739F...` | Coinbase Verified Country |
| `0x379e23de...` | Base (8453) | `0x357458739F...` | Coinbase One Membership |

#### `soulbound_token` — Non-Transferable Tokens

Soulbound tokens (SBTs) per ERC-5192 are non-transferable NFTs that represent permanent credentials — DAO membership, course completion, professional certification.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `credentialType` | string | Yes | `"soulbound_token"` |
| `chainId` | integer | Yes | EVM chain ID |
| `contract` | string | Yes | SBT contract address |
| `tokenStandard` | string | No | `"ERC-5192"`, `"ERC-4973"`, etc. |
| `label` | string | Yes | Human-readable credential description |
| `met` | boolean | Yes | Whether the wallet holds the SBT |
| `conditionHash` | string | Yes | `0x`-prefixed SHA-256 hash of the canonical condition |
| `blockNumber` | string | Yes | Hex-encoded block number at time of check |
| `blockTimestamp` | string | Yes | ISO 8601 timestamp of the block |

#### Extensibility

New credential types (e.g., Verifiable Credentials anchored on-chain, Polygon ID proofs) can be added by defining a new `credentialType` string and its associated fields. Consuming agents MUST ignore credential types they do not recognize.

### 3.3 Verification Flow

A consuming agent verifies an `onchain_credentials` signal without trusting the presenting agent:

```
1. Extract `provider.jwks` URL from the signal
2. Fetch the JWKS document (cacheable, 24h TTL)
   GET https://insumermodel.com/.well-known/jwks.json
   -> { "keys": [{ "kty": "EC", "crv": "P-256", "x": "...", "y": "...", "kid": "insumer-attest-v1" }] }

3. Find the key matching `provider.kid`
4. Reconstruct the signed payload:
   payload = canonical_json({
     "type": "onchain_credentials",
     "binding": { ... },
     "credentials": [ ... ]
   })

5. Verify ECDSA P-256 signature:
   verify(provider.sig, payload, public_key) == true

6. Check freshness:
   if now() > expiresAt AND consumer requires fresh data:
     re-query the provider
```

If verification succeeds, the consuming agent knows the credential results are authentic and were checked at the stated time, regardless of who presented the signal.

### 3.4 Composability

On-chain credentials can serve as **hard gates** before other signals are evaluated:

```
policy:
  require:
    onchain_credentials:
      - credentialType: eas_attestation
        schemaUid: "0xf8b05c79..."    # Coinbase Verified Account
        met: true
  then:
    effective_trust = w1 * vouch_score + w2 * behavioral_score
```

This prevents the Trojan agent attack identified by @lorenzocipriani-huawei — an agent cannot accumulate behavioral trust to bypass a hard credential requirement. Credentials are the floor; behavioral and vouch scores determine the ceiling.

### 4.2 Trust Profile Dimensions

Activity signals are organized into dimensions, each with `passCount`, `failCount`, and `total` fields indicating how many checks passed. Consuming agents compute a dimensional score as `passCount / total` (0.0–1.0). InsumerAPI currently provides four dimensions:

#### `stablecoins` — Economic Commitment

Presence of stablecoins (USDC across multiple chains). A wallet holding stablecoins demonstrates active economic participation and a minimum level of capital commitment.

**Relevance weighting:** High for financial delegations (DeFi swaps, payment processing). Low for informational tasks.

#### `governance` — Protocol Participation

Holdings of governance tokens (UNI, AAVE, ARB, OP). Governance token holders participate in protocol decision-making and have a vested interest in ecosystem health.

**Relevance weighting:** High for DAO governance tasks, protocol integration decisions. Medium for general-purpose delegations.

#### `nfts` — Community Membership

Ownership of NFT collections, particularly blue-chip or membership collections. NFT holdings can indicate community standing, early adoption, or specific access rights.

**Relevance weighting:** High for NFT marketplace tasks, community-gated delegations. Low for financial tasks.

#### `staking` — Protocol Security Participation

Holdings of liquid staking tokens (stETH via Lido, rETH via Rocket Pool, cbETH via Coinbase). Staking token holders have committed ETH to network security, signalling long-term ecosystem alignment.

**Relevance weighting:** High for infrastructure delegations (validator coordination, protocol security). Medium for DeFi delegations. Low for NFT and marketplace tasks.

### 4.3 Task-Contextual Scoring

The API returns raw pass/fail counts per dimension — it does not compute a composite score. Consuming agents compute their own task-specific score from the dimensional data:

```
dimension_score = passCount / total    (0.0–1.0 per dimension)

task_score = w_stablecoins * stablecoins_score
           + w_governance  * governance_score
           + w_nfts        * nfts_score
           + w_staking     * staking_score

where weights are set by the consuming agent per task type
```

**Example task-contextual weights:**

| Task Type | Stablecoins | Governance | NFTs | Staking |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DeFi swap delegation | 0.5 | 0.3 | 0.1 | 0.1 |
| NFT marketplace listing | 0.1 | 0.1 | 0.7 | 0.1 |
| DAO proposal submission | 0.2 | 0.6 | 0.1 | 0.1 |
| Infrastructure delegation | 0.2 | 0.2 | 0.1 | 0.5 |
| General-purpose research | 0.25 | 0.25 | 0.25 | 0.25 |

### 4.4 Optional: Merkle Storage Proofs

For high-value delegations where the consuming agent requires trustless verification without relying on the provider's signature, `onchain_activity` signals MAY include EIP-1186 Merkle storage proofs:

```json
{
  "type": "onchain_activity",
  "binding": { ... },
  "trustProfile": { ... },
  "merkleProofs": [
    {
      "chainId": 1,
      "contract": "0xa0b86991c6218b36c1d19d4a2e9eb0ce3606eb48",
      "label": "USDC on Ethereum",
      "blockNumber": "0x1257a07",
      "blockHash": "0xabc...",
      "storageProof": {
        "key": "0x...",
        "value": "0x...",
        "proof": ["0x...", "0x...", "0x..."]
      },
      "accountProof": ["0x...", "0x...", "0x..."]
    }
  ],
  "provider": { ... }
}
```

The consuming agent verifies the proof against the block hash (obtainable from any Ethereum node) to confirm the raw storage value. This eliminates trust in the provider entirely — the proof is a mathematical fact about the blockchain state at a specific block.

Merkle proofs are available on a subset of EVM chains. They are not available for all chains or Solana.

### 4.5 Verification Flow

Same as `onchain_credentials` (Section 3.3) — fetch JWKS, find key by `kid`, verify ECDSA signature over the payload. For Merkle proofs, additionally:

```
1. Obtain the block hash for merkleProofs[i].blockNumber from a trusted Ethereum node
2. Verify accountProof against the block's state root
3. Verify storageProof against the account's storage root
4. Decode the storage value to confirm the balance
```

### 4.6 Freshness and Staleness

On-chain activity changes with every block. The `profiledAt` + `expiresAt` model gives consuming agents control:

| Delegation Type | Recommended Max Age |
|---|---|
| Financial operations (DeFi, payments) | 60 seconds |
| Write-access delegation | 300 seconds (5 min) |
| Read-only delegation | 3600 seconds (1 hour) |
| Discovery/browsing | 86400 seconds (24 hours) |

If a signal is staler than the consumer's tolerance, the consumer SHOULD re-query the provider rather than rejecting the agent outright.

## 6. Composite Trust Formula

The full trust formula integrating all four signal types:

```
effective_trust = gate(credentials) * (w1 * vouch + w2 * behavioral + w3 * activity)
```

Where:

- `gate(credentials)` = 1 if all required `onchain_credentials` pass, 0 otherwise
- `vouch` = vouch chain score (0.0–1.0)
- `behavioral` = behavioral score (0.0–1.0)
- `activity` = task-weighted `onchain_activity` score, computed from `passCount / total` per dimension (0.0–1.0)
- `w1 + w2 + w3 = 1.0`, weights set by consuming agent per task

The credential gate is a hard requirement — if the agent lacks required credentials, the trust score is zero regardless of behavioral history or vouch chains. This prevents the Trojan agent pattern where an agent accumulates social trust to bypass credential requirements.

### 6.1 Progressive Trust Tiers

| Tier | Required Signals | Suitable For |
|---|---|---|
| **Tier 0 — Anonymous** | None | Public read-only queries |
| **Tier 1 — Identified** | `onchain_activity` (any score) | Low-risk delegations, discovery |
| **Tier 2 — Verified** | `onchain_credentials` (EAS attestation) | Medium-risk delegations |
| **Tier 3 — Trusted** | `onchain_credentials` + `vouch_chain` + `behavioral > 0.7` | High-risk delegations, financial operations |

## 8. Security Considerations

### 8.1 Signature Replay

Attestation signatures include the wallet address, conditions, and timestamp in the signed payload. Replaying a signature for a different wallet or condition set will fail verification. The `expiresAt` timestamp provides temporal replay protection — consumers SHOULD reject signals past their expiry.

### 8.2 Key Rotation

Providers rotate keys by publishing new keys in their JWKS endpoint with a new `kid`. Old keys are retained during a transition period. Consumers SHOULD cache JWKS for no more than 24 hours.

### 8.3 Provider Trust

The `provider.jwks` URL is a trust anchor. Consuming agents MUST fetch JWKS over HTTPS and SHOULD pin known provider JWKS URLs. A compromised provider JWKS would allow forged attestations — this is the same trust model as TLS certificate authorities.

For maximum trust, consuming agents can verify on-chain state directly (via their own RPC node) rather than relying on provider attestations. Merkle storage proofs (Section 4.4) provide a middle ground — the proof is verifiable against public block headers without trusting the provider.

### 8.4 Privacy

- `onchain_credentials` signals expose credential existence (pass/fail), not the underlying data (e.g., a Coinbase Verified Account attestation confirms verification without revealing personal information)
- `onchain_activity` signals expose boolean holdings (`met: true/false`) per dimension, not raw balances, unless Merkle proofs are requested
- Consuming agents SHOULD NOT store trust signals beyond their TTL

---

## 9. Supported Chains

On-chain signals are available across **32 chains**: 30 EVM + Solana + XRPL.

**30 EVM chains:** Ethereum, Base, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, BNB Chain, Avalanche, Chiliz, Soneium, Plume, World Chain, Sonic, Gnosis, Mantle, Scroll, Linea, zkSync Era, Blast, Taiko, Ronin, Celo, Moonbeam, Moonriver, Viction, opBNB, Unichain, Ink, Sei, Berachain, ApeChain.

**Solana:** SPL token balances and NFT ownership.

**XRPL:** Native XRP, trust line tokens (RLUSD, USDC via Circle), and NFTs. XRPL wallets use r-address format and are passed via the `xrplWallet` request parameter rather than a CAIP-2 `wallet` + `chainId` pair.

Chain identifiers follow [CAIP-2](https://github.com/ChainAgnostic/CAIPs/blob/main/CAIPs/caip-2.md) format: `eip155:{chainId}` for EVM chains, `solana:5eykt4UsFv8P8NJdTREpY1vzqKqZKvdp` for Solana mainnet.

Merkle storage proofs and EAS attestation verification are available on 11 RPC-connected EVM chains. Not available on Covalent-only chains, Solana, or XRPL.']

I completely agree that a cron-like approach is only one option. For example, in the current proposal, we lack the functionality to:

## Main idea  
Provide an *optional*, standardized protocol for scheduling tasks — just as HTTP servers aren’t required to implement every HTTP method, but standards exist for all of them.

## Use cases  
- **Daily reminder**: “Remind me every day about something.”  
- **Hourly polling**: “Every hour, poll API\xa0X for a value and, if a condition is met, perform an action.”  
- **Monthly reports**: “Each month, gather reports from several sources and notify the user only when attention is needed.”

## Challenges

### 1. Unintended service overuse  
- Any public-facing endpoint could be targeted for DDoS attacks.  
- Agent‑to‑agent (A2A) scheduling isn’t limited to external services; large internal systems with many agents may have an even greater need.  
- Developers should implement rate limits in LLM‑based apps (to control token costs); the same safeguards apply to scheduled tasks.

### 2. Scalability  
- The scheduler is the only stateful component; running agents don’t need to track future tasks.  
- From an agent’s perspective, executing a scheduled task is identical to handling a newly created task from an endpoint.  
- A simple implementation could have the scheduler invoke the same endpoint that agents use — only done automatically. More sophisticated designs might introduce message queues to ensure tasks aren’t lost.

### 3. Developer time  
- Scheduling is an *optional* feature.  
- The market will decide what features are valuable; many users may welcome the ability to “fire and forget” repetitive jobs by defining them once.  
- Without standardization, each developer would waste time reinventing scheduling solutions.

I worry that this approach undermines our goal of a unified protocol — but I may have misunderstood. Please share detailed, real‑world implementation scenarios so we can compare and refine both proposals.']

In order to more effectively describe the A2A protocol in a consistent way across different protocols, this PR refactors the specification to describe the application protocol in a transport agnostic way, and then have separate sections that describe how each of the transports map to the abstract application protocol.  To see a preview of what it looks like you can go here https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/

The goal of the TSC is to use the changes in this PR as the baseline for a v1.0 Release Candidate. This will give SDK maintainers an stable document to validate the changes in the specification through implementations before v1.0 release.

There are many pending feature requests for the A2A specifications that the TSC are supportive of.  However, getting a stable, consistent, unambiguous, multi-protocol specification is necessary before additional features can be added safely.

## Document Restructuring 

- [A2A Operations](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#3-a2a-protocol-operations) are described independent of wire protocol 
- [Protocol Data Model](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#4-protocol-data-model) is described using protobuf as source of truth. All other serializations are derived from that. 
- Protocol bindings (formerly described as transports) are now described in their own sections
  - [JSON-RPC](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#9-json-rpc-protocol-binding)
  - [gRPC](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#10-grpc-protocol-binding)
  - [HTTP](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#11-httpjsonrest-protocol-binding)
- [Operation Parameters ](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#32-operation-parameter-objects) describe structures reused across different operations
- [Operation Semantics](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#33-operation-semantics) describe common behavior patterns across operations

## New Sections

- [Requirements Language](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#21-requirements-language) 
- [Capability Validation](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#334-capability-validation)
- [Abstract description of error handling](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#332-error-handling)
- [Abstract description of "headers"](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#325-headers)
- [Extensions](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#46-extensions)
- [Versioning](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#36-versioning)
- [Custom Binding Guidelines](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#12-custom-binding-guidelines)
- [JSON Field Naming Conventions](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#54-json-field-naming-convention)
- [Data Type Conventions](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#55-data-type-conventions)
- [Security Considerations](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#77-security-considerations)
- [Agent Card Signing](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#84-agent-card-signing)
- [IANA Considerations](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#13-iana-considerations)

## Protocol Clarifications

- Defining order for events returned from [Stream Message](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#312-stream-message)
- [JSON Examples](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#416-filepart) provided for protobuf definitions of data model objects that previously used discriminators

  - [JSON-RPC](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#94-error-handling)

As @darrelmiller  mentioned, any system that groups the agents or interacts with these agents should anyway be able to identify trusted vs. malicious agents relying on agent signature or any other mechanisms whether an id is specified or not specified.

Since id is an attribute of agent card and is included part of the serialized agent card to generate the signature, the signature does validate the id as well.', "### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Currently Agent Card does not have a unique identifier attribute for an agent. `agent_card.name` is not guaranteed unique and is prone to branding changes.



### Describe the solution you'd like

- Add a new`id` attribute to the agent card which must be a randomly generated UUID.
- This `id` must remain same for all versions of an agent.
- Mark the `id` as optional for backward compatibility.
- Clients can reliably use `id` as the identifier if set in the agent card.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

### Code of Conduct

- [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct", "I've already discussed this with @kthota-g and I agree that this field is useful, but putting some of the points I raised in this issue for posterity:

Could a system that cares about continuity for versions just use a compound identifier of `{AgentCard.provider.url} + '/' + {AgentCard.name}`? That should be sufficiently unique. Noted drawback: this makes it harder to change `name` and `provider.url` fields. Given `name` is the only display name for the agent, if you put, e.g., branding in the agent name and wanted to change that it'll break the identifier.

Alternatively, we just indicate that the name field should be unique and repurpose that field. One pattern we use in [aip.dev](https://google.aip.dev/148) is that `name` is the unique identifier, and `display_name` is for people. Display names should probably be able to be localized, too (i.e. repeated with a lang string attached). Noted drawback: we've already established that the `name` field contains display name-like strings, so changing it now could be disruptive.

One concern I have with using identifiers for tracking versions of an agent over time is that it requires you strongly trust the content of the AgentCard. If I were able to get an AgentCard into such a system that points to a malicious agent, but has the same `id` and a high `version` value as another agent, the system would group them together and claim my malicious agent is the most recent version. And if the system uses other heuristics to detect if agents should be grouped (served on the same domain, have the same provider, etc.), is the identifier still needed?

AgentCard signatures can help with this, but you'd need some means of binding the signing key on the signature to the `id` field. A super cheap version of this that is kinda nice is to make the agent identifier a JWK thumbprint of the public key (or just the public key bytes, I suppose) used for a signature. The identifier isn't super readable at that point, but it's definitely possible to tie to a signature."]

['## Summary

Official A2A tutorials show inconsistent discovery endpoint paths across different protocol versions without clarifying which version they target. This causes clients to look for the wrong endpoint file when connecting to agents.

## Problem Description

Multiple conflicting endpoint paths are used across documentation:

| Source | Endpoint Path | Protocol Version | Issue |
|--------|--------------|------------------|-------|
| v1.0 spec | `/.well-known/agent-card.json` | v1.0 | ✅ Correct |
| v0.3.0 spec | `/.well-known/agent-card.json` | v0.3.0 | ✅ Correct |
| v0.2.x spec | `/.well-known/agent.json` | v0.2.0-0.2.6 | ✅ Correct |
| Python SDK Tutorial | `/.well-known/agent.json` | **Not specified** | ⚠️ Missing version context |
| .NET SDK Tutorial | `/.well-known/agent.json` | v0.2.1 mentioned | ⚠️ Should clarify version-specific |
| Java Sample | `/.well-known/agent-card` | **Not specified** | ❌ Missing `.json` extension |

## URLs Affected

### Official A2A Documentation:

1. **Python Tutorial**: https://a2aprotocol.ai/docs/guide/google-a2a-python-sdk-tutorial
   - Uses: `/.well-known/agent.json`
   - Issue: No protocol version specified in tutorial

2. **.NET SDK Tutorial**: https://a2aprotocol.ai/docs/guide/a2a-dotnet-sdk
   - Uses: `/.well-known/agent.json`
   - States: v0.2.1
   - Issue: Should note this is v0.2.x specific

3. **Java Sample**: https://a2aprotocol.ai/docs/guide/a2a-java-sample
   - Uses: `/.well-known/agent-card` (missing `.json` extension)
   - Issue: No protocol version specified, wrong path format

## Specification Reference

**Official Protocol Specifications:**

- **v0.2.x**: `/.well-known/agent.json`
- **v0.3.0+**: `/.well-known/agent-card.json`

Sources:
- v0.2.x: https://a2a-protocol.org/v0.2.0/specification/
- v0.3.0: https://a2a-protocol.org/v0.3.0/specification/
- v1.0: https://a2a-protocol.org/dev/specification/

## Impact

### Client Connection Failures
Clients following Python tutorial will look for `agent.json` when connecting to v0.3.0+ agents that expose `agent-card.json`, causing discovery to fail.

### Implementation Confusion
Developers are unsure which endpoint to implement:
- Should I expose `agent.json` or `agent-card.json`?
- What's the difference between protocol versions?
- When did the endpoint name change?

### Cross-Version Incompatibility
Agents implementing v0.3.0 won't be discoverable by clients following v0.2.x tutorials that don't attempt fallback.

## Examples

### Example 1: Python Tutorial (Missing Version Context)
**URL**: https://a2aprotocol.ai/docs/guide/google-a2a-python-sdk-tutorial

**Code Shown**:
```python
# Discover the agent
agent_card_url = f"{agent_url}/.well-known/agent.json"
response = requests.get(agent_card_url)
agent_card = response.json()
```

**Issue**: Tutorial doesn't specify this is v0.2.x only

### Example 2: Java Sample (Wrong Path Format)
**URL**: https://a2aprotocol.ai/docs/guide/a2a-java-sample

**Code Shown**:
```java
String discoveryUrl = agentUrl + "/.well-known/agent-card";  // Missing .json
```

**Issues**:
1. Missing `.json` extension
2. No protocol version specified
3. Unclear if this is v0.3.0 or v1.0

## Recommended Fix

### For Tutorial Authors

1. **Add Protocol Version Badge** at top of each tutorial:
   ```markdown
   > 📋 This tutorial targets **A2A Protocol v0.2.6**
   ```

2. **Specify Endpoint Clearly**:
   ```markdown
   ## Discovery Endpoint

   **v0.2.x**: `/.well-known/agent.json`
   **v0.3.0+**: `/.well-known/agent-card.json`

   This tutorial uses v0.2.6, so we'll use `agent.json`.
   ```

3. **Show Fallback Pattern** for clients:
   ```python
   # Try v0.3.0+ first
   try:
       response = requests.get(f"{agent_url}/.well-known/agent-card.json")
       if response.status_code == 200:
           return response.json()
   except:
       pass

   # Fallback to v0.2.x
   response = requests.get(f"{agent_url}/.well-known/agent.json")
   return response.json()
   ```

### For Java Sample

Fix the path to include `.json` extension:
```java
String discoveryUrl = agentUrl + "/.well-known/agent-card.json";
```

## Additional Context

This inconsistency was discovered while implementing multi-version A2A client support. The client attempted to discover agents using tutorial code but failed when connecting to v0.3.0 agents.

## Related Issues

- #1104 - AgentCard version field inconsistency
- #1365 - "kind" vs "type" discriminator inconsistency

## Specification References

1. **A2A Protocol v0.2.6**: https://a2a-protocol.org/v0.2.0/specification/
   - Discovery Endpoint: `/.well-known/agent.json`

2. **A2A Protocol v0.3.0**: https://a2a-protocol.org/v0.3.0/specification/
   - Discovery Endpoint: `/.well-known/agent-card.json`

3. **A2A Protocol v1.0**: https://a2a-protocol.org/dev/specification/
   - Discovery Endpoint: `/.well-known/agent-card.json`', "Be sure that you're using the version of the a2a-sdk which supports protocol version `0.2.5` (`a2a-sdk>=0.2.10`)

Both the client and the server agent must be following protocol version `0.2.5` or higher for this to work.

(The versions currently aren't in sync between the SDK and the protocol, but this should be resolved in 0.3.0)", "> Be sure that you're using the version of the a2a-sdk which supports protocol version `0.2.5` (`a2a-sdk>=0.2.10`)
> 
> Both the client and the server agent must be following protocol version `0.2.5` or higher for this to work.
> 
> (The versions currently aren't in sync between the SDK and the protocol, but this should be resolved in 0.3.0)

Name: 36_signature_signatures_agentcard_jws
Representative_Docs:
['One of my primary desires was that I wanted to embed these signatures into the AgentCard directly, rather than either:

- Have an alternate representation of an AgentCard that's wrapped in a signing envelope
- Pass around signatures separately from AgentCards

The property that someone can pass around an AgentCard document directly and it contains the information necessary to verify it is nice, and that you don't need to be aware of a separate form of the document that wraps the AgentCard.

JWS was convenient since there's an established means of passing around signatures with "detached" payloads. At least a few of the libraries I checked out even have support for this directly. It's not clear to me if there's a similarly established means for DSSE. I didn't want to invent something new here, and I also didn't like the idea of embedding a signature that duplicates the entire AgentCard (i.e. the AgentCard contains a signature envelope which has a payload which is... the AgentCard).

The other convenient (but controversial?) aspect of JWS is the protocol-defined properties that can be used to indicate the keys used to verify the signature. Again, I didn't want to make anything new if I could get away with it. I believe the Sigstore bundle format helps serve that purpose, since it contains the x.509 cert. So, DSSE alone doesn't seem sufficient, we'd need something additional.

Sigstore seems like a great option that has a ton of useful properties, but I didn't want to require something like "if you want to sign AgentCards you must adopt Sigstore", or "if you want to verify signatures you must be aware of Sigstore". The choice for model developers like NVIDIA to adopt it makes sense, but our situation as an open protocol is a bit different: when we make choices like this, we're not putting requirements on ourselves, we're putting requirements on everyone that uses A2A. We must do that for the protocol to be effective, but I think you have to spend those "requirement tokens" judiciously. I'm open to the position that this is one of those cases, FWIW.

I also want users who are using Sigstore to get its benefits, so I'd love to find a way to make that possible. My ideal would be that an AgentCard producer using Sigstore can add signatures that a verifier not using Sigstore can still verify.', "### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

There is no means to verify the integrity of an AgentCard. It is not possible for a party to attest to the content of an AgentCard.

Consumers of AgentCards may require the ability to know that an AgentCard is unchanged from when it was retrieved from a particular source, such as from a registry.

Consumers of AgentCards may require that AgentCards are vetted by a trusted source.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Allow AgentCards to contain signatures. This allows consumers to verify that the content of an AgentCard is unchanged since the signature was added. Signatures should be presented in a well-known format: I propose JSON Web Signatures (JWS). This allows verifiers to leverage pre-existing libraries for performing verification.

Signatures should cover the content of the AgentCard and also be contained by the AgentCard. That is, an AgentCard should get ` signatures` field that contains a list of signatures. This allows the AgentCard to be passed around as a single document that includes information sufficient to verify the integrity.

For a more complete description of the solution, see: https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/discussions/199#discussioncomment-13770576

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- Signatures via HTTP headers: there exists a standard for HTTP message signing. This could be used to return signatures for an AgentCard when served by an AgentCard endpoint. However, the signatures are not then contained within the AgentCard data and are tied to the transport mechanism (HTTP). We'd prefer a self-contained solution.

- Out-of-band signing: we could define a separate process for retrieving signatures of an AgentCard. This could be protocol-defined, where verifiers understand the specific means of retrieving known signatures for an AgentCard, such as from the rekor ledger offered by Sigstore. This allows great flexibility, but increases the burden on verifiers to understand external systems.

- AgentCard JWTs: rather than attaching signatures to an AgentCard, we could instead treat an AgentCard as a JWT. This format is similar to the proposal, however it inverts the relationship between AgentCard and signature: rather than an AgentCard containing a signature, the JWT contains the AgentCard. This eliminates the need to define a specialized process for producing signing input, however it bifurcates the serving format for signed and unsigned AgentCards. This means every consumer must concern themselves with whether an AgentCard is served as a JSON payload or as a JWT -- we either introduce a separate means of serving AgentCard JWTs, which increases the surface area of the protocol, or we require every implementer to handle both formats.

- Sign at registries: we could omit signatures from AgentCards, but expect that in production scenarios AgentCards are served via a registry that packages AgentCards with signatures. This effectively removes signing from the core A2A protocol and puts it off onto other registry/discovery protocols. We believe signing is a valuable feature, and so standardizing it via the core A2A protocol is appropriate.

### Additional context

See https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/discussions/199.

### Code of Conduct

- [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct", 'Alright so a month later and I've had time to try to work up a proposal.

I had a few thoughts based on the discussions here and elsewhere:

1. Signatures directly on the AgentCard (rather than out-of-band) provide a much more direct way for users to understand how to find and verify signatures. Out-of-band signatures are still possible, of course -- I can't stop you from doing it!
2. Signatures should be optional, and adding them should be backwards compatible. This means we don't fundamentally change what is returned from an AgentCard endpoint -- not directly serving an envelope-wrapped AgentCard.
3. The format should be familiar (meaning: not novel, leveraging existing standards) and lightweight.
4. We should be able to leverage existing libraries in every major language to assist in the verification process
5. Adopting signatures should be simple and not require major new infrastructure/systems buy in. But leveraging systems like sigstore should be possible.

Those desires led me to a pretty straightforward option: [JSON Web Signatures (JWS)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7515).

So, here's the proposal. Please let me know if you believe this would solve what you're looking for with signed agent cards.

# **A2A: Agent Card Signing**

## *mikeas@ / Draft: 2025-07-14*

## *Public* 

# **Overview**

We propose adding signatures to the AgentCard to allow verifying the integrity of the AgentCard content. This is an optional feature of AgentCards. We will use the standard JSON Web Signatures (JWS) format for representing the signature. Trust in the signature can be established via standard JWS fields that indicate the source of keys used to create the signature.

# **AgentCard Signature**

We will extend the AgentCard to include a `signatures` field. This field will store a list of JWS JSON objects with detached payload. This adheres to the [RFC 7515 specification](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7515#section-3.2) for JSON Web Signatures, and [RFC 7797 specification](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7797#section-5.3) for detached payloads. The following is the approximate typescript definition of the signature type:

```ts
interface JSONWebSignature {
  // The JWS protected header. A base-64 encoded JSON object containing JWS header values. This value is included
  // in the signing payload, therefore it is protected from alteration.
  protected: string;
  // The base64-encoded signature, computed according to the algorithm specified in the JWS header.
  signature: string;
  // The unprotected JWS header. This contains information for applications interpreting the signature, but
  // is not included in the signature and therefore can be tampered with.
  header?: { [string]: string };
}
```

**Alternative:** We could collapse the signature down to a single string by using the compact serialization format with a detached payload. All header values would need to be placed in the protected header for this to work. The resulting signature is a string of the form `<b64-protected-header>..<b64-signature>` (note the 2 sequential dots, which is the format for a JWS with a detached payload). This format can be slightly more compact compared to the object version if unprotected headers are not used. I initially did not choose this format since I am biased towards preferring structured formats over string formats, but this format is common and well supported.

A full AgentCard example that includes signatures might look like this:

```ts
{
  "protocolVersion": "0.2.9",
  "name": "GeoSpatial Route Planner Agent",
  "description": "Provides advanced route planning, traffic analysis, and custom map generation services. This agent can calculate optimal routes, estimate travel times considering real-time traffic, and create personalized maps with points of interest.",
  "url": "https://georoute-agent.example.com/a2a/v1",
  "preferredTransport": "JSONRPC",
  "additionalInterfaces" : [
    {"url": "https://georoute-agent.example.com/a2a/grpc", "transport": "GRPC"},
    {"url": "https://georoute-agent.example.com/a2a/json", "transport": "HTTP+JSON"}
  ],
  "provider": {
    "organization": "Example Geo Services Inc.",
    "url": "https://www.examplegeoservices.com"
  },
  "iconUrl": "https://georoute-agent.example.com/icon.png",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "documentationUrl": "https://docs.examplegeoservices.com/georoute-agent/api",
  "capabilities": {
    "streaming": true,
    "pushNotifications": true,
    "stateTransitionHistory": false
  },
  "securitySchemes": {
    "google": {
      "type": "openIdConnect",
      "openIdConnectUrl": "https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration"
    }
  },
  "security": [{ "google": ["openid", "profile", "email"] }],
  "defaultInputModes": ["application/json", "text/plain"],
  "defaultOutputModes": ["application/json", "image/png"],
  "skills": [
    {
      "id": "route-optimizer-traffic",
      "name": "Traffic-Aware Route Optimizer",
      "description": "Calculates the optimal driving route between two or more locations, taking into account real-time traffic conditions, road closures, and user preferences (e.g., avoid tolls, prefer highways).",
      "tags": ["maps", "routing", "navigation", "directions", "traffic"],

        "Plan a route from '1600 Amphitheatre Parkway, Mountain View, CA' to 'San Francisco International Airport' avoiding tolls.",
        "{\"origin\": {\"lat\": 37.422, \"lng\": -122.084}, \"destination\": {\"lat\": 37.7749, \"lng\": -122.4194}, \"preferences\": [\"avoid_ferries\"]}"
      ],
      "inputModes": ["application/json", "text/plain"],
      "outputModes": [
        "application/json",
        "application/vnd.geo+json",
        "text/html"
      ]
    },
    {

      "name": "Personalized Map Generator",
      "description": "Creates custom map images or interactive map views based on user-defined points of interest, routes, and style preferences. Can overlay data layers.",
      "tags": ["maps", "customization", "visualization", "cartography"],
      "examples": [
        "Generate a map of my upcoming road trip with all planned stops highlighted.",
        "Show me a map visualizing all coffee shops within a 1-mile radius of my current location."
      ],
      "inputModes": ["application/json"],
      "outputModes": [
        "image/png",
        "image/jpeg",
        "application/json",
        "text/html"
      ]
    }
  ],
  "supportsAuthenticatedExtendedCard": true
  //////// Key addition:
  "signatures": [
    {
      "protected": "eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpPU0UiLCJraWQiOiJrZXktMSIsImprdSI6Imh0dHBzOi8vZXhhbXBsZS5jb20vYWdlbnQvandrcy5qc29uIn0",
      "signature": "QFdkNLNszlGj3z3u0YQGt_T9LixY3qtdQpZmsTdDHDe3fXV9y9-B3m2-XgCpzuhiLt8E0tV6HXoZKHv4GtHgKQ"
    }
```
